gbekrc.text: Some attacks this week didn't need much of a trick. A fake support call, a trusted extension, a shared link, or a device with no password. Small things that people barely think about. Yet each was enough to cause serious trouble. Then there were the bigger messes. Billions stolen, hidden networks of hacked devices, poisoned software, and attackers finding new ways to turn normal tools against their users. Even the places meant to keep money and systems safe ended up with problems of their own. The strange part is how often the damage started somewhere nobody was looking. And that's before getting to the long list of fresh bugs, shady services, and scams making the rounds. Quite a bit to sort through. Here's what made the list. ⚡ Threat of the Week N. Korea Sets New Record with Binance $6.43B Crypto Theft — The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance to a North Korean hacking group called TraderTraitor. The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin. Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism. 🔔 Top News Volt Typhoon Uses Covert Silent Train Network in 0-Day Attacks — Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon has been using a framework that relies on rotating chains of connected devices compromised on demand, including to facilitate zero-day attacks targeting high-value systems. It's codenamed Silent Train because the threat actor uses it against select targets, cleans it up after each operation to minimize detection and attribution, and refreshes it continuously. Silent Train is a relay infrastructure formed of compromised devices to hide the origin of its attacks. The findings highlight evidence of efforts to pre-position access within what it described as "strategic communications, critical infrastructure and other ecosystems that become essential during geopolitical tensions or crises." Silent Train is built around "rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices." The nature of these victims "indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region." Polymarket Briefly Suspended Trading After Third-Party Hack — Prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily suspended trading after hackers compromised DebugBear, a third-party service, to distribute cryptocurrency-draining JavaScript that siphoned approximately $2.7 million in assets from 33 deposit wallets in under an hour. "Our DNS server records were compromised through our domain registrar. We are currently unable to receive emails sent to our domain," DebugBear said in an update shared on October 31, 2026. "Based on our initial investigation this attack targeted the website of a specific customer. We have not seen any indication of a compromise of our internal systems, though we will continue to investigate this." In June, Polymarket disclosed another third-party compromise that injected a malicious script into its frontend, leading to reported losses of around $3 million. Shared ChatGPT Links Lead to Code Execution — Researchers from Parameter Labs disclosed a now-patched flaw in ChatGPT that turned an ordinary share link into an attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. "An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," Parameter Labs said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session." Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation, and send data from that conversation to an external server. Official Claude Code Extension on Cursor Marketplace with SSH Backdoor — Two versions of the Claude Code extension distributed through Cursor Marketplace were tampered with to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems. Cursor said the incident impacted up to 5,000 users. In response to the incident, Cursor said it rotated its keys, rebuilt the marketplace, and worked with the cloud provider to take the server offline so that the reverse shell is no longer functional. It also stressed that no other extensions were maliciously modified as part of the attack. However, several questions surrounding the supply chain attack remain unanswered, including how the threat actor managed to publish a malicious extension under Anthropic's name on Cursor's marketplace and what level of access they were able to obtain. FBI Seizes bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine — The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) announced the seizure of a domain associated with a bulletproof hosting provider (BPH) named Virtualine. The DoJ said the service was being used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity, including "the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults and minors, and international money laundering designed to conceal and promote criminal conduct. However, the long-term impact of such crackdowns has been questioned. According to Intel 471, disruptions have driven customers to newer services operated by former resellers, fragmenting the market rather than eliminating demand. The disclosure comes as the Australian Signals Directorate said it gained backend access to Amadey's operations and severed its access to 180,000 computers across the globe. Keystone to Destroy 18,835 Hardware Wallets — Keystone confirmed a security incident involving its official website where an attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party data monitoring tool to escalate privileges and obtain some customer information and a key used to verify the authenticity of our devices. This included 25,964 records containing names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order information, along with 12,873 checkout records containing names, contact details, and shipping information submitted by users. Besides stopping the use of the old key, Keystone plans to destroy 18,835 devices in existing inventory that contain the old key. "Shipping of all unshipped orders from our official website has been suspended," it said. "Sales will switch to a preorder model until production of devices using the new key is complete, after which shipping will resume." In a related development, another hardware cryptocurrency wallet maker Trezor said it received credible reports about a suspected hardware crypto-theft implant in a Trezor Safe 5 sold by its reseller CryptoBilis in Southeast Asia. "If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onwards and are using it to store funds, please move your funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed as soon as possible," it said. uCreator Android Spyware Can Clone WeChat Accounts — A commercial Android spyware offering called uCreator is designed to target ordinary users of mobile wallets and messaging applications across China and Southeast Asia, including GCash (Philippines), WeChat, WeCom, QQ, Telegram, WhatsApp, LINE, Zalo, KakaoTalk, Viber, and MoMo. It can also be used to clone WeChat accounts. Victims install repackaged copies of legitimate applications disturbed through sideloading or social engineering flows. The attack leverages a variation of on-device virtualization techniques observed in malware like GodFather to conduct fraud. "GodFather spins the banking app up inside a virtual container and drops a fake overlay on top to phish credentials: the victim is really typing into the attacker's screen," security researcher Ovi Liber said. "uCreator shares the substrate but it draws no overlay. This is a case really of overlay-the-app versus instrument-the-app, with the second being quieter and also not being confined to a login screen. As an operator, it scales to any app the vendor writes a module for." Gheist Turns GitHub Actions into a Secret Extraction Service — An automated campaign dubbed Gheist has been observed planting a secret-dumping workflow named "sync-check" in every repository that stolen GitHub tokens can reach. "The workflow seeks to print the repository's secrets into its own workflow log," Wiz said. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later." The Google-owned cloud security company said it recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts. The campaign was first detected in mid-September 2026. ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. "On command, the bot opens hundreds to thousands of TCP connections to a target chosen by the operator and keeps them open for the requested duration, sending a single near-empty keepalive byte every few seconds," Nozomi Networks said. "Initial access came through Telnet, using the default credentials (user root, empty password). It was first observed by Group-IB on January 7, 2026. k4wmho.text: A botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes, lost control of its servers in late October in a takedown led by Google. Google says it is highly confident that device maker Videostrong intentionally put a backdoor in the boxes and sold access to criminals. They used the boxes for ad fraud and to pass other people's internet traffic through owners' home connections. The backdoor is still on the boxes, and owners cannot remove it themselves. Videostrong, based in Shenzhen, China, makes Android TV boxes and other devices under its own name and for other brands. The backdoor, called x.cpe, was built into many device models and brands over several years. Google does not believe a rogue insider or a mistake was to blame. Google used legal action to take down the domains and servers that controlled the botnet. It also took down the control domains of more than a dozen malware families loaded through the backdoor. Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI worked with Google on the operation. Because the criminals behind that malware also spread it in other ways, Google expects the action to cut off their access to at least 10 million more infected devices. It warns that backdoor operators and the criminals who buy from them quickly switch to new tools when one part of their setup is disrupted. Google has cut ties with Videostrong. It banned the company, and any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices and from supplying software to other certified device makers. What the Backdoor Did The x.cpe backdoor runs as a system app inside the firmware, with system-level access, according to Google's analysis. It reports to the botnet's command-and-control (C2) servers and waits for orders. To install software silently, it first turns off the app checks in Google Play Protect, Android's built-in security feature. Through the backdoor, the botnet's operators could install apps without the owner knowing, run commands, capture the screen and map the network the box sits on. Google says it saw Videostrong's operators use some of these powers. They took live screenshots, sent keystrokes, copied out account details, device information, app lists and system logs, and opened reverse shells, which give a remote command line into the box. Most of the criminals' modules, the add-on programs loaded through the backdoor, turned the boxes into residential proxies or sold their spare bandwidth. A residential proxy service sells access to a home internet connection, so a customer's traffic appears to come from an ordinary household. Other modules faked views of online ads. Most infected devices are Android TV set-top boxes, but the backdoor also turned up on telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signage. TrendAI, Trend Micro's enterprise business unit, counted 1,472,554 infected devices across 206 models between June 3 and October 1, and says the real number is at least that high. Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan had the most. The U.S., Germany, the U.K., Australia and Canada each had about 26,000 to 42,000. What Owners Can Do Synthient, which tracks proxy networks and botnets, has published a list of 182 device model names seen in the campaign. The list warns that a model name alone does not confirm that a box is infected. Synthient's report focuses on MECOOL-branded boxes, which it links to Videostrong. It bought a MECOOL KM9PRO Max and found the backdoor preinstalled. Plume, which makes Wi-Fi software for internet providers, found more than a dozen different devices using the botnet's control server, most of them from MECOOL. Because x.cpe is part of the firmware, removing it does not stick. It reinstalls itself when the box restarts. TrendAI says the backdoor runs as a system app signed with the maker's key, so cleanup needs "vendor action, platform protection or replacement of the device." Plume recommends a full factory reset, because the modules may have installed more backdoors, but it does not say whether a reset removes x.cpe itself. Synthient goes further, telling consumers to throw the boxes away for good because they pose a high risk of malware. For organizations, Synthient recommends these steps: Use its published indicators to find MECOOL or similar devices on the network. Disconnect and throw away any that turn up. Block the control domains and IP addresses its report lists. Keep other smart devices on separate network segments, away from sensitive systems. TrendAI advises companies with remote staff to treat unmanaged consumer devices on home networks as part of their attack surface, and to keep corporate access behind managed devices. How Videostrong Was Identified In Google's account, x.cpe passes settings from the C2 server to other Videostrong apps, including its YokaTV Player streaming app. One of the GitHub accounts that hosted the botnet's packages is named yf-videostrong. Synthient, which worked with Google, also concluded with high confidence that Videostrong runs the operation. It points to a document signed by Videostrong's research and development director in an open folder on one of the botnet's servers, and to a Videostrong web domain that shares an IP address with the operators' control panel. Plume found that Videostrong supplies both the firmware for these devices and tools to manage them remotely. A Gap in Google's Device Tests Google requires device makers to go through a set of compatibility and security tests. It says Videostrong hid its code to bypass a gap in those tests and loaded the malicious code after a device's first boot. Google has changed its review process and is improving its checks of the firmware on certified Android TV devices. As of November 2, Videostrong's own website listed products it calls "Google Certified Android TV Box" and "Google Certified Android TV Stick." Plume says the botnet included both Google-certified devices and devices running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) version. Google's report does not say how many certified devices were affected. When Google sued over the BadBox 2.0 botnet in July 2025, the more than 10 million devices involved were uncertified.

cfv172.text: The maintainer of BTCPay Server, an open-source cryptocurrency payment processor, has urged users to install the latest version as hackers have been draining “hot wallets” on instances running older versions. Operators were initially advised to shut down their servers pending a full investigation into the unauthorized Bitcoin and Litecoin payments. The BTCPay Server project provides businesses with a self-hosted payment processing solution that allows them to accept Bitcoin and other digital assets directly into their own wallets, eliminating payment intermediaries or paying platform processing fees. It handles checkout invoices and payment verification, including payments over the Lightning Network. Early Monday, the maintainer said it had “identified an attack vector targeting instances running version 2.4.1 (July 23, 2026) or earlier” and strongly urged users to update to version 2.4.7. BTCPay founder Nicolas Dorier said the attacks did not target public servers. The investigation focused on determining how the threat actor was able to log in as an administrator to instances running versions older than 2.4.2. On October 29, the company disclosed a critical vulnerability discovered via Anthropic’s Frontier OSS scanner, which prompted the release of version 2.4.7 as an emergency security update. However, Dorier said that there were clues that the attacker used vulnerabilities in BTCPay Server versions earlier than 2.4.2, released on August 7, which the project later confirmed. “Our incident response investigation identified an attack vector targeting instances running versions 2.4.1 (Jul 23, 2026) or older,” BTCPay Server says. “We have no credible reports of hot wallet drains for users running the latest 2.4.7 release. We again urge everyone to keep their BTCPay Server updated.” The BTCPay project began receiving reports of theft yesterday evening (UTC) and responded by asking VPS hosting providers to take affected server instances offline as a precaution to protect customers. In a security alert today, the project maintainer said that it is currently responding to affected users and continues to receive incident reports. Users who lost funds as a result of the recent attacks are asked to send details to security@btcpayserver.org, and to report the losses to local authorities. qkjefs.text: In 2024, AT&T lost sensitive communication logs of 109 million customers in a massive data breach. Call logs can reveal a lot about you, like your closest relationships, where you live and work, and your daily routine. 109 million people (nearly a third of Americans) suffered a massive data breach in April 2024 that exposed their AT&T communication logs. AT&T lost sensitive information including phone numbers, call and text counts, call durations, and location data from May to October 2022, and January 2023, meaning the data was approximately two years old at the time of the breach, impacting both current and former customers. AT&T said the records didn’t contain call content, customer names, or Social Security numbers. That’s less reassuring than it sounds, because even on their own, call logs reveal a lot about you. What are call logs? Every call, text, and data session generates records inside your carrier’s network. The two kinds that matter here are: SIP messages. Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) manages calls and texts, both within a carrier and between networks. One message starts a session and another ends it. Carriers use them mainly to troubleshoot dropped calls and failed texts. Call Detail Records (CDRs). CDRs summarize each call, text, and data session: who was involved, when, for how long, and often which cell site your phone used. Carriers use them for billing and for settling charges with roaming partners. Anyone with access to your call logs can identify your closest relationships, locate your home and workplace, and reconstruct your daily routine in more detail than you could yourself. If you called an oncologist a few years ago, there’s likely a record of it, how long you talked, and where you were. If you texted an old friend afterwards, there’s a log of that too. Call metadata can even be correlated with publicly available information to derive identities. Malte Spitz showed how far this goes. In 2011 he sued his telecom for the data it held on him, received roughly 35,000 records, and reconstructed a strikingly specific replay of several years of his activities. Why call logs are easy to get Three things make them an easy target. They’re kept for a long time. Most carriers don’t say how long. Privacy policies typically promise to retain data for “as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes” of the policy. In 2022, responding to a request from the FCC chair, carriers disclosed that they kept geolocation data for as long as five years, far longer than phone service requires. One reason is to monetize it. They sit in a few big targets. Carrier data is frequently breached. AT&T was one of many Snowflake customers hit by credential-based thefts, alongside Ticketmaster and Neiman Marcus. Salt Typhoon, the China-linked campaign, reportedly compromised every major US carrier, which could put call metadata for any American within reach. They have other buyers. Retained logs are used to build detailed behavioral profiles that are sold to ad networks and data brokers and, in some cases, handed to the government. The AT&T breach is the predictable result. The records were available to steal because they existed. Protect yourself with private cell service. 11bvteq.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq by an Iran state-aligned threat actor between August and October 2026. According to a report published by Dream Research Labs, the campaign has led to the compromise of a high-profile individual in Israel, along with additional compromises affecting a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region. The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq. It exhibits no technical overlap with other known hacking groups. Attacks mounted by the group are known to rely on spear-phishing as an initial access pathway to lure recipients into opening trojanized utilities or clicking on attacker-controlled websites that host similar tools as direct downloads. Previous attack chains documented by Elastic Security Labs and Group-IB have led to the deployment of SHELBYLOADER (aka HOTAIR), which is launched via DLL sideloading to ultimately execute a backdoor called SHELBYC2 (aka AEROSTAT) that uses GitHub for command-and-control (C2), data exfiltration, and remote control. Elastic is tracking the threat cluster under the moniker REF8685. Then early last month, Palo Alto Networks shed light on a campaign dubbed Blinder Tunnel in which the threat actor, which it calls CL-STA-1178, was observed masquerading as the Dubai Airports IT department to distribute malware-laced coding challenges to high-value targets. The bogus recruitment scheme was first detected in late March 2026, although evidence indicates that the attackers were staging and testing attack infrastructure as far back as November 2025. The social engineering campaign is assessed to have approached specific targets with lucrative job offers to trick them into executing a self-contained application that mimicked a career portal and instructed them to complete a questionnaire. Submitting the questionnaire does not cause any data to be exfiltrated or initiate any response from an external domain. Instead, it's meant to serve as a harmless decoy and build credibility before delivering the next stage payload containing the malware in the form of a Microsoft Visual Studio project archive that's dressed up as a coding assessment. The attack chain makes use of three techniques to establish persistent access: A malicious C# project ".csproj" file is used to trigger AppDomainManager injection, followed by DLL sideloading to deliver an updated version of SHELBYLOADER (aka ShelbyLoader V2), which then launches SHELBYC2. Also deployed via SHELBYC2 is a tunneling utility called Blackwood. "The attackers behind the activity used tailored social engineering techniques to masquerade as Dubai Airports recruiters, using a trojanized Visual Studio coding challenge to target a high-value job seeker based in Iraq," Unit 42 said. "The campaign is characterized by misuse of built-in developer tools and DLL sideloading. Attackers also used AppDomainManager hijacking to bypass security monitors like ETW [Event Tracing for Windows]." The latest findings from Dream show that the threat actor continues to rely on social engineering, while combining both credential phishing and malware delivery. This involves the use of government, webmail, and cloud-service lookalike domains to collect credentials or present attacker-controlled file downloads. Some of the highlighted domains include - gcc-sg[.]cloud/owa/auth/logon.aspx mfakuwait[.]online/owa/auth/logon.aspx moelcloud[.]online/drive/file/d/1JpH3ySmJpvX6TyGnF7C-S8qYiaoxyC5O The threat actor has also been observed setting decoy brand domains for a fake videoconferencing application called StarkMeet (stark-meet[.]com, stark-meet[.]online, and stark-meet[.]website). Installing and launching the app leads to the execution of ShelbyLoader V2 and SHELBYC2. The development is also a sign that the threat actor is trying out different methods for malware delivery, ranging from coding assessments to counterfeit software. Dream said the DarkBlinders activity belongs to the same operational cluster as UNC5795 and Dust Specter, citing infrastructure and malware overlaps. Dust Specter, documented by Zscaler in March 2026, refers to a suspected Iran-nexus operation targeting government officials in Iraq by impersonating the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. "Historical server fingerprints, overlapping victimology, and supporting attribution research lead us to assess with medium confidence that UNC5795 and UNC5187 may represent related sub-clusters within the broader APT34 group," it added. "Their overlapping focus on Iraqi government entities adds context to this technical connection and suggests a shared intelligence collection interest. Combined with their respective APT34 associations, these findings support a medium-confidence assessment that the two clusters are operationally related and may belong to the same broader group." Prince of Persia Hosts C2 in the U.S. for the First Time in a Decade The disclosure comes as Prince of Persia (aka Infy), a lesser-known threat group sponsored by the Iranian government, has been observed running one of its C2 servers ("68.65.122[.]203") from the U.S. this year. The server was likely built in July 2026. The infrastructure is a second-stage C2 server associated with Tornado, a Tonnerre variant that's dropped via one-day software vulnerabilities and uses both HTTPS and the Telegram API for C2. The emergence of new C2 servers in late May 2026 follows three months of inactivity, which has been described as the "longest downtime in nearly two decades of activity by the threat actor." "We have been monitoring Prince of Persia's exfiltration activity for the past six months," Tomer Bar, associate vice president of security research at Semperis, said. "The number of victims remains low, which could indicate either targeted attacks or difficulties infecting new victims." "The Iranian threat actor decided to host its new C2 server on U.S. soil — at the same time as the beginning of the recent hostilities between Iran and the United States. This is the last place we expected to find the threat actor hiding."

93jqmr.text: A cyberattack on refrigeration systems has disrupted stores run by multiple supermarket chains across several European countries after hackers remotely changed temperature settings on freezers and cooling systems. In some cases, hackers shut down refrigerators or activated defrosting systems, causing temperatures to rise, resulting in significant product losses and forcing store managers to intervene early in the morning. Refrigeration failures were identified at dozens of supermarkets, but it is unclear whether they were hit in a coordinated attack or targeted individually. More than 115 stores in Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Estonia have been affected. Spokespersons for multiple chains confirmed the issues in statements for BleepingComputer. Supermarket chains that acknowledged refrigeration issues include: ICA (Sweden) - At least 4 locations affected Coop (Sweden) - 7 locations confirmed affected Ahold Delhaize (Belgium and Luxembourg) - Around 40 locations affected Carrefour (Belgium) - 15 locations affected Spar Colruyt (Belgium) - 5 locations affected Intermarché (Belgium) - Around 15 locations affected SuperValu (Ireland) - 13 stores Selver (Estonia) - 1 store In the Netherlands, at least 17 butcher shops and neighborhood stores have been affected. Additional stores are dealing with the same problems in Belgium, including an Ikea superstore in Mons, grocery stores, and chocoloate shops. Spokespersons for ICA, Ahold Delhaize, and Spar Colruyt told BleepingComputer that their companies are providing support to affected stores and working to resolve the situation. “We can confirm that we have been informed of an incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network,” stated ICA’s press officer. “The incident impacted the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation.” A representative of the Colruyt Group told BleepingComputer that "there is an impact on the refrigeration systems at around five Spar stores." "These stores are operated by independent entrepreneurs who have their own refrigeration systems. We are currently doing everything we can to resolve the issue." In a statement for BleepingComputer, Ahold Delhaize stated that refrigeration systems at several dozen stores have been impacted by an IT incident. “We have identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen stores,” the company's communications department said, adding that the company "immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational." A spokesperson for Coop, one of the largest grocery store chains in Sweden, said that refrigeration units at a small number of stores were impacted, and in once case the system started to generate heat. "We can confirm that a small number of stores were affected overnight into Monday - specifically 7 out of more than 800 stores," Coop told BleepingComputer. "The situation is currently contained and under control. The issues have ranged from completely shut-down refrigerators and freezers to partially functioning units, and in one case, the system beginning to generate heat." In Belgium, only Carrefour stores in two regions were affected, and all hypermarkets remained completely operational. "The impact at Carrefour is very limited: currently 15 of our 700 stores are affected, both in Flanders and Wallonia," Carrefour stated. "Not a single hypermarket is among them. All stores remain open because it only concerns a few refrigeration units, mainly freezers. Quick action was taken so that all stores can stay open." An ICA store manager told TV4 that temperature settings had been changed overnight to +50°C (122°F) and could not be modified, forcing the store to discard frozen food. According to RTL media publication, Ahold Delhaize warned managers by SMS around 4 a.m. about refrigeration issues, and some stores used refrigerated trucks to try to preserve stock. The publication also identified Sabcobel as the vendor of refrigeration systems across several of the impacted locations. According to Sabcobel's director, Stephan Moelans, the attacker leveraged the same vulnerability used in similar attacks last month in France. Moelans said that technicians started disconnecting affected installations since 1a.m. and attributed the disruption to remotely activated defrost functions. Although the company tried to protect customer's systems, a simple software update is not enough, as refrigerators also require physical modifications. "The simplest solution is to manage the refrigerators via a secure internet connection. Most of our clients have adopted this solution since the attack in France," Moelans told RTL. BleepingComputer has contacted Sabcobel to learn more about the incident and its level of involvement, but we are still waiting for a response. Last month's refrigerator attacks in France impacted hundreds of stores using Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC and Copeland/Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers that were compromised by remote attackers who set them to defrost mode. 1jr16tz.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 02, 2026Vulnerability / Artificial Intelligence Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code, IBM said last week. Langflow is an open-source tool for building AI agents and workflows, and its vulnerability reports go to IBM. Every release from 1.0.0 through 1.12.8 has the flaws, and the only fix is version 1.13.0. Neither flaw is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, as of the catalog's October 30 update. Six other Langflow flaws are listed there, most recently CVE-2026-9198, which was added in August. The four Langflow flaws in IBM's bulletin, first published on October 28 and updated the next day, are: CVE CVSS score (IBM) Account needed What IBM says it could allow CVE-2026-93680 9.8 (Critical) No Bypassing security restrictions, because of improper authentication CVE-2026-110186 9.8 (Critical) No Running arbitrary code, because of improper control of code generation CVE-2026-110193 8.8 (High) Yes, a low-privileged account Making the Agentic Assistant generate or submit component code that runs operating system commands on the server CVE-2026-110192 6.5 (Medium) Yes Getting sensitive information from insufficiently protected credentials One of the flaws is "unauthenticated remote code execution exploitable through model context protocol tool enumeration," according to IBM. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Langflow can offer its flows as tools to AI apps that support MCP. A module in the public Metasploit Framework already cites CVE-2026-93680, the authentication bypass. It connects to a Langflow server's MCP endpoint without credentials, starts a session, and lists the tools the server offers. It does not run code or commands on the server. Its author lists Langflow 1.5.0 through 1.11.4 as affected, a narrower range than IBM's. When automatic login is enabled, Langflow logs users in as superusers without prompting them to sign in. The setting LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN is enabled by default in Langflow 1.12.8. Its code description warns that it "bypasses authentication and should only be used in development environments." The module was tested on Langflow 1.8.4 with automatic login turned on. Another of the four flaws is "an incomplete remediation of an auto-login security control," according to IBM. The bulletin does not say whether servers with automatic login turned off are vulnerable. Upgrading to 1.13.0 Langflow 1.13.0 came out on October 22. Version 1.12.8, released the same day, still has the flaws, and PyPI lists no later 1.12 release as of November 2. IBM offers no workaround for servers that cannot upgrade yet. Langflow 1.13 turns automatic login off by default. To upgrade: Back up the database, the secret key and uploaded files. If the server uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in, as Langflow's upgrade guidance describes. Upgrade the Python package with pip install --upgrade "langflow==1.13.0". For Docker, move to the langflowai/langflow:1.13.0 image and keep the deployment's persistent data. If you cannot sign in after upgrading, follow the recovery steps that the same guidance links to. Do not delete or reinstall Langflow to get access back, because Langflow's documentation warns this can permanently remove your flows. On October 29, IBM also published CVE records for 29 other Langflow flaws and named versions 1.12.4 and 1.12.5 as their fixes. One of them, CVE-2026-104339, could also let an attacker with no account run arbitrary code, and IBM rates it 9.8. None of the 33 records, these four included, lists 1.13.0 as affected.

mgox6z.text: Forty percent of security teams now use AI every day, and another 56% are testing it. Only 4% have no plans to adopt it, according to Prophet Security's State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey of more than 250 CISOs, SOC leaders and practitioners. For the teams still testing, the next decision is whether their own SOC is ready. AI SOC readiness has two parts: whether a SOC has the problems AI SOC agents are built for, and whether it has the data access, context, written standards and oversight rules that AI agents need to investigate alerts accurately in its environment. A SOC does not need to be far along a maturity model to be ready. AI agents do their first work on the bottom layer, alert handling, and the analyst hours they return give a team room to work on the layers above it. The next section describes those problems. Technical readiness covers four areas: access and context, an investigation standard with baseline metrics, rules for what the agent may do, and a plan for the time it gives back. Which SOCs benefit the most from AI SOC agents The SOCs that gain the most from AI SOC agents usually recognize several of the problems below, whether an outside provider works their alerts or their own analysts do. If an MDR or MSSP works your alerts: Your MDR flags threats too slowly. The provider works your alerts in a queue it shares with its other customers, so the escalation for a real intrusion can arrive hours after the activity started. Your MDR hands alerts back for lack of context. An escalation arrives with a short summary and questions such as is this login expected, is this a production server, or is this user traveling? The provider often does not know your users, assets and business well enough to finish the investigation, so your analysts do the rest. Your MDR closes alerts without showing its work. When the provider marks an alert benign, the note may not say what it checked and how it came to that conclusion, so your team either trusts the call or runs the investigation again. Your MDR's coverage stops at the tools it supports. Many contracts cover the EDR and a set list of log sources, so alerts from everything else, such as a SaaS application or a second cloud platform, land on your team. If your own analysts work the queue, including whatever the provider sends back: "Are we impacted?" takes days to answer. When a critical vulnerability or a new campaign makes the news, leadership wants an answer the same day. Getting one means hunting across the environment by hand, usually by an analyst who is also working the queue. Lower-severity alerts wait or get closed in bulk. A thorough investigation means pivoting across the SIEM, EDR, identity provider, cloud console and email tools, so the team keeps up with critical and high alerts and gets to the rest when it can. In the survey, 60% of respondents said an alert they had ignored or missed later turned into a serious issue, such as a breach or downtime. Noisy detections get switched off. Tuning a rule that fires too often takes time the team does not have, so the rule gets disabled and the technique it watched goes uncovered. Hunting and detection engineering wait for spare time. Proactive work happens when someone has a free afternoon, because the alert queue comes first. A few senior analysts carry the hard cases. Only one or two people know how to work the most difficult investigations, so a single resignation can set the team back. Nights and weekends are thinly covered. Staffing the queue around the clock takes more analysts than the budget covers, so alerts that fire after hours wait until morning or go to whoever is on call. AI SOC agents are built for this work. They are designed to start on each alert as it arrives, whichever tool raised it and at whatever hour. They can pull the context an outside provider lacks from your own systems and record the evidence behind each conclusion, so your team can check it. Some can also run a hunt the day a new threat is disclosed, which turns "are we impacted?" into a set of queries with answers. The analyst hours they return can go to the detection and hunting work that waits today. If several of these problems sound familiar, the need is there. The next question is whether your SOC can support a deployment. Where AI agents fit on a SOC maturity model Prophet Security's SOC maturity model, the SOC Hierarchy of Needs, has five levels: alert management, detection coverage, threat awareness, proactive hunting and posture improvements. Each level depends on the one below it. A team buried in alerts rarely gets to hunting, and a team that hunts without threat awareness has no clear idea what to look for. Many SOCs have not yet stabilized the first level. In the State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey, respondents said 28% of their alerts are never investigated. AI SOC agents usually start at that first level, investigating alerts as they arrive. Newer platforms also run hunts and propose detections, work that reaches into levels two and four. Either way, the analyst hours they return go to work above the first level, so readiness depends on what the first level needs. An AI agent can only investigate what it can query An AI agent investigates by running queries against your tools, so it cannot see anything it has no access to. If it can query the EDR but not the identity provider, it can describe what happened on the endpoint but not which account was behind it. Readiness here has three parts: API access to the sources an investigation needs. That usually means the SIEM, EDR, identity provider, cloud platforms, email and key SaaS applications. Context the agent can read. An agent needs asset criticality, user roles, VIP lists, business units and known-benign activity, such as scheduled scans and admin scripts, to tell an attacker from a legitimate administrator. Healthy data pipelines. A silent or delayed log source can make an investigation look complete when key evidence is missing, so the health of the pipelines that feed investigations needs monitoring. A quick test: take five recent incidents and list every query a senior analyst ran to close them. Any query the agent could not run marks a gap to close before a pilot. Data access also raises the most common objection. In our survey, 44% of teams cited data privacy and how AI models are trained, the most frequent roadblock respondents named. Ask each vendor whether your data trains their models and where your data is processed. Define a finished investigation and record your baseline A pilot needs a written standard to grade the agent against. In many SOCs, only senior analysts know that standard, and it is rarely written down. The standard covers which evidence closes a phishing case, when an impossible-travel alert needs a call to the user's manager, and what counts as enough to call an alert benign. Writing it down for your highest-volume alert types also gives new analysts an onboarding document. Also keep a list of the detections that were switched off. In our survey, up to 40% of organizations had turned off some detections because they lacked the people to check them. When an agent investigates every alert, some of those rules can come back, and the list tells you where to start. Then record the numbers you will compare against: the share of alerts investigated, mean time to investigate, time from alert to first look, and how often closed alerts are reopened. The survey gives a reference point. A thorough investigation takes an average of 75 minutes, and alerts often wait close to an hour before anyone opens them. You can download our guide on detection engineering to learn more about how an agentic SOC benefits detection engineering. Decide what the agent may do, and who approves more Investigation and action carry different risks, and most teams treat them differently. In the survey, 57% of teams require a human to review every AI decision before an alert is closed. On response, 44% have AI recommend actions that people carry out, 30% let it handle low-risk remediation on its own, and no respondent gives it full, unsupervised autonomy. A ready SOC has these rules written down before a pilot starts: Default approvals. A list of the actions that stay human-approved, such as isolating a host, disabling an account or blocking a domain. How permissions widen. Who can grant the agent more autonomy for a category of action, and what track record they need to see first. Where findings land. Agent findings should appear in the case management or ticketing tools analysts already use, so nobody has to watch another console. Who owns feedback. A named person reviews the agent's mistakes and turns corrections into guidance it will use next time. Starting with read-only access for investigations, then widening permissions as confidence grows, applies the same rules a SOC uses for a new human analyst. Prophet Security's framework for building trust in an AI SOC follows the same stepwise approach. A readiness checklist mapped to the maturity model Answer each question yes or no. Part 1 checks the need, and Part 2 checks technical readiness. The level in parentheses shows which layer of the SOC Hierarchy of Needs each item belongs to. Part 1: Does your SOC need AI SOC agents? Do escalations from your MDR or MSSP arrive hours after the activity started? (Level 1: alert management) Does your provider hand alerts back because it lacked the context to finish them? (Level 3: threat awareness) Does your provider close alerts without showing what it checked? (Level 1: alert management) Do alerts from tools outside your provider's coverage land on your team? (Level 1: alert management) Does it take more than a day to tell leadership whether you are impacted by a new vulnerability or campaign? (Level 4: proactive hunting) Do low- and medium-severity alerts wait, or get closed in bulk without an investigation? (Level 1: alert management) Have noisy detections been switched off because no one had time to tune them? (Level 2: detection coverage) Do hunting and detection engineering wait until someone has spare time? (Level 4: proactive hunting) Do only one or two senior analysts know how to work your hardest cases? (Level 1: alert management) Do alerts that fire at night or on weekends wait until morning? (Level 1: alert management) Each yes is a problem an AI SOC agent can take on, and the more yes answers, the stronger the case for a deployment. Part 2: Is your SOC ready to deploy them? Can a new tool query your SIEM, EDR, identity, cloud and email sources through an API? (Level 1: alert management) Are asset criticality, user roles and known-benign activity recorded somewhere a system can read? (Level 3: threat awareness) Is there a written standard for what a complete investigation includes, for the alert types that make up most of your volume? (Level 1: alert management) Have you decided which actions stay human-approved, and who can widen the agent's permissions? (Level 1: alert management) Do you monitor whether the log sources your investigations depend on are arriving? (Level 2: detection coverage) Do you know your current share of alerts investigated and your mean time to investigate? (Level 1: alert management) Do you keep a list of detections that were switched off for capacity reasons? (Level 2: detection coverage) Is there a plan, with named owners, for the analyst hours an agent will return, such as scheduled hunts or detection work? (Level 4: proactive hunting) A "no" on any of the first four is worth fixing before a production pilot. The other four can be worked on during it. What to do if the answer is not yet Most items on the Part 2 list are configuration and documentation work: issuing API credentials, exporting asset and user context, and writing down the investigation standard. A workable order: Close the access gaps from the five-incident test first, since every later step depends on the agent seeing the data. Write the investigation standards for your highest-volume alert types. Run the agent in parallel with your analysts for a few weeks. Record the baseline before it starts, and treat every analyst override as data about where the agent needs more context. Widen the agent's permissions one category of action at a time, as its record supports it. Some teams that are not ready consider building their own agents instead. The survey suggests caution: 72% of AI users had tried building internal AI tools, and 46% of those projects were abandoned, never reached production, or were replaced by a commercial product. Building a functioning prototype is only a small chunk of the work. Most of the work is engineering and maintenance of integrations that take weeks to build but break when a vendor changes an API; rate limits to work around; model deprecations every six to nine months that force a full round of evals, guardrails, and prompt injection testing; and audit trails explaining why each alert was closed. How Prophet Security Works Prophet Security is the leading AI SOC platforms for enterprise SOCs, recognized in Rising in Cyber 2026, an honor voted on by more than 150 CISOs and security leaders. Its platform, Prophet AI, works from the stack a team already runs. First-generation AI SOC tools stopped at alert triage. Prophet AI enables an agentic SOC, with specialist agents for investigation, threat hunting and detection engineering. Prophet AI SOC Analyst investigates every alert at every severity, around the clock, with the depth of a senior analyst. It queries SIEM, EDR, identity, cloud and email tools directly and records every question, query and piece of evidence behind a determination, so an analyst can rerun any query and check the work. It takes response actions only within permissions the customer sets, with human approval as the default. Prophet AI Threat Hunter is built to answer "are we impacted?" It keeps a profile of each organization's industry, technology stack and the threat actors that target it. When a severe new threat emerges, hunts for it run automatically in the background. Scheduled hunts, including hunts against coverage gaps and questions the team writes in plain language, run on the cadence the team sets. Suspicious leads go to the SOC Analyst for a full investigation. Prophet AI Detection Engineer takes on the detection engineering work that waits for spare time. It keeps a live MITRE ATT&CK coverage map built from the organization's own investigations, showing which techniques are covered, which have gone quiet and which are dark. It builds and tunes detections from what investigations, hunts and coverage gaps reveal, writes them in the rule language of the SIEM or tool they run in, and backtests each one against the organization's own history. Each change arrives as a reviewable proposal with its rationale and backtest results, and by default nothing reaches production until the team approves it. Each product's findings feed the others. Investigations show which detections are noisy and where coverage is thin, hunts look in those gaps, and what the hunts find becomes new detections. The team teaches Prophet AI in plain language, and that guidance shapes how investigations run, how hunts are scoped and how detections are written. Customer data never trains its models, and the data plane can run inside the customer's own VPC. The full State of AI in Security Operations 2026 report, including the survey data cited here, is available to download.

u52t7u.text: Attackers posing as IT support on Microsoft Teams talked employees into giving them remote control of their PCs. They then used insecure Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) settings to obtain login certificates for privileged accounts, including one for a domain controller. Microsoft said in a report that it investigated two such intrusions, one of which resulted in company data being copied to an external server. The attackers exploited no flaw in Teams itself. They relied on social engineering and on AD CS that had been set up insecurely, and Microsoft did not tie the activity to any known group. How the Attacks Began Both intrusions started the same way, Microsoft said. The attackers messaged and called employees on Teams while posing as the company's own IT or help desk, working from outside tenants with support-themed names so the contact looked familiar. They talked each user into opening Quick Assist, a remote-help tool built into Windows, and reading the connection code back to them. That gave the attacker direct, hands-on control of the workstation. From there, the attacker dropped an archive into the Downloads folder, unpacked it into a new folder named to resemble a Windows update, and ran its contents with a portable Python, Bun, or Java runtime. File names alone were a weak signal, because one copy was renamed while still carrying the real runtime's version details. What a Certificate Buys an Attacker AD CS is the Windows role that issues the certificates users and computers present when they log in. A certificate from a poorly configured template lets whoever holds it sign in as the account it names. Microsoft said such a certificate continues to work even after the account's password is reset or the first machine is wiped, so neither step ends the attacker's access. Case 1: Privileged Certificates, and a Gap in Containment In the first intrusion, the attackers found a certificate template with a weakness known as ESC1. With that kind of template, the requester can name the account the certificate will represent, so a low-privileged user can request one that stands in for a privileged account. The first wave of calls targeted three users and one workstation, producing certificates for three highly privileged accounts. Microsoft Defender's automatic attack disruption cut those identities off and dropped their active sessions. One privileged account, though, had been left out of the automatic response, so it stayed usable. About 90 minutes later, a larger wave hit 16 users and a second workstation, producing certificates for 8 more privileged accounts. Microsoft said more than 1,000 later attempts to reach files over SMB or to log in were blocked. Within seconds of obtaining a certificate, the attacker signed in to a domain controller and ran DCSync, a tool for copying password data from Active Directory. The operation had already begun when containment took hold, limiting how much could be replicated. Microsoft did not say how much credential data the attacker obtained. The excluded account was the opening. The attacker kept using it, reached a file server, and ran a renamed copy of the file-copying tool Rclone to move data from a share to an outside SFTP server. Microsoft did not say how much data was taken. The case shows, in Microsoft's words, that "partial identity containment can reduce attack activity while still leaving a viable privileged route." Case 2: A Certificate for the Domain Controller The second intrusion began the same way but took a different direction because that template weakness was not present. The attacker instead used a technique called PetitPotam to force a domain controller to authenticate to a machine the attacker controlled. That NTLM login was relayed to the AD CS web enrollment page, an abuse known as ESC8, with no password needed. The attacker used the relayed login to request a certificate for the domain controller itself. With that certificate and Kerberos (PKINIT), the attacker obtained a ticket-granting ticket for the domain controller, turning a one-off relayed login into a lasting identity. Here the response held. Defender raised ESC8 alerts, the customer isolated the workstation, and Microsoft said no further activity followed. The difference between the two came down to containment. In the first, automatic disruption blocked most of the attack, but the one excluded account stayed open. In the second, isolating a single workstation stopped it. What Defenders Can Do There is no patch, because nothing here was a software flaw. Microsoft's advice is about configuration and response. Have staff confirm any unexpected support request through a known internal channel before sharing a screen or handing over remote control. Limit which outside Teams tenants can reach employees, and allow only approved remote-support tools. Review sign-in certificate templates for ones that let the requester name the account, or that too many users can enroll in, and remove enrollment rights that are not needed. Require HTTPS and turn on Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on web enrollment endpoints, and turn off NTLM there where you can. Microsoft's KB5005413 covers this, and its Defender for Identity posture checks flag templates and endpoints exposed to ESC1 and ESC8. Turn on certificate auditing. If a bad certificate was issued, revoke it, but remember that revocation does not cancel Kerberos tickets already issued; review active tickets separately. Treat any account left out of automatic containment as a deliberate decision and assign a manual action in its place. What Is and Isn't Known Microsoft did not attribute the intrusions to any named group and did not give the dates on which they happened. The methods are not new. Researchers named the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate weaknesses in 2021, and the PetitPotam coercion trick was disclosed the same year. Microsoft itself had documented the Teams help-desk-to-remote-access entry method earlier in 2026. What this report adds is that the two techniques meet in real intrusions, along with the lesson about the excluded account. Newer Windows is less exposed to the ESC8 step. Microsoft turned EPA on by default for AD CS in Windows Server 2025, whereas Server 2022 and 2019 require it to be enabled manually. Indicators and Detections Microsoft's report lists Defender alerts across Teams, endpoints, and identity signals, and four advanced hunting queries that it calls "starting points for investigation" rather than proof on their own. It also published three file hashes tied to the initial-access scripts: SHA-256 85b6c424117494d3056e88689dbc94c75e9afdb187a339714043aec0da109f17 (JavaScript initial-access script) SHA-256 f326201269f1ee2f803ae435317507263bb6e0dbfdeb70bd1bb5446e2e46f001 (Python initial-access script) SHA-256 06c5c14f043aee3bcc5843b5f50909623d5c9a6239a7c1fba9cddad4111469e7 (Python initial-access script)

1pwvgn8.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign specifically targeting Linux infrastructure associated with government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure. The activity, observed by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 between October 2025 and April 2026, has been tracked under the moniker CL-UNK-1211, where "CL" refers to cluster and "UNK" stands for unknown motivation. A notable aspect of the campaign concerns the use of large language models (LLMs) and/or automated artificial intelligence (AI) agents to generate payloads and execute malicious code. "The attackers behind this cluster of activity focused on Linux environments to conduct extensive reconnaissance and maintain persistent network access to support intelligence-gathering," researchers Roey Porat and Tom Fakterman said. "The attackers attempted to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to access social media accounts." The campaign employs a "versatile operational playbook," leveraging a combination of open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors, and web shells to maintain access. Another hallmark involves attempts to disable endpoint protections, wipe system logs, and plant deceptive red-team markers so as to disguise the activity as a legitimate security assessment. The threat actor has also been observed using malicious PHP and shell scripts, likely generated using AI, to maintain persistence, perform reconnaissance, and exfiltrate data. "Rather than standard developer documentation, multiple scripts contained conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the code's logic to the operator who provided the initial instructions," the cybersecurity company said. "Their presence suggests that the code was either copied directly from an AI prompt output or deployed by an automated AI agent." A mix of open-source and bespoke PHP web shells is used as a way to maintain a persistent backdoor into the host networks. The access is then abused to gather credentials from the targeted environment using three different methods - Replacing the .bashrc file with a malicious version containing a command to steal passwords. Injecting code into PHP login pages to harvest admin credentials. Scanning for cleartext email, SMTP, and database passwords within configuration files and command history files. Also deployed as part of the attacks is a custom, multi-platform remote access trojan written in Go that supports various persistence methods to maintain long-term access on Windows and Linux systems. Called SysGoRAT, it establishes a command-and-control (C2) connection over WebSocket to a hard-coded IP address ("104.194.158[.]65:443") and fetches seven types of commands - command, to execute arbitrary commands via /bin/sh -c (Linux) or cmd /C (Windows) control, to spawn via sub-commands an interactive shell (shell_start), screenshots (screenshot), exfiltrate files to the C2 server (download), and install persistence (persist) list_dir, to list directory content shell_input, to create an interactive shell session proxy_connect, to establish a TCP connection to an arbitrary target proxy_data, to relay data bidirectionally to an established proxy connection proxy_close, to terminate and remove a proxy session Furthermore, the attacks make use of in-memory reverse shells to avoid leaving forensic artifacts on disk, as well as enumerate "/var/qmail/mailnames/" directories to count the number of emails stored in specific folders. "Next, the attackers searched for social media-related emails," Unit 42 explained. "They deployed a PHP script, named search_social.php, that searched for specific keywords in email headers and displayed the results in a user-friendly format." "The script then parsed the response and displayed the exact file path, social media account email sender, recipient and subject." The attackers have also been found attempting to generate a bash script named "zip_mails.sh" in a bid to compress emails of interest into ZIP archives and exfiltrate the information. However, syntax errors present in the script meant that the program failed upon execution. "This campaign demonstrates how attackers are combining traditional post-exploitation techniques with AI-accelerated workflows to target governmental Linux server infrastructure," Unit 42 said. "By leveraging AI to rapidly generate, adapt and deploy operational scripts, the attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 maintained a fast pace of operation while minimizing manual developer overhead." The development comes as Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, along with Microsoft, documented threat actors' abuse of open-source agentic penetration testing frameworks like ARTEX, PentAGI, Hexstrike, and CAIRN to carry out a "broad range of actions" across various stages of the attack life cycle at an unprecedented speed and scale. Although ARTEX was taken down by its author after reports of widespread misuse emerged, it has spawned multiple versions, including a commercial offering dubbed ARTEX PRO and a localized variation called ScopeWeaver. Some of the cases are listed below - Use of ARTEX by Storm-0940 (aka UNC7228) to orchestrate data theft campaigns targeting entities in the U.S. and Europe across the enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor manufacturing and design, and telecommunications industry verticals. Use of ARTEX by financially motivated threat actors to facilitate data theft extortion, including the targeting of the financial sector in Asia. Use of ARTEX by North Korean state-sponsored hacking groups like Onyx Sleet (aka Andariel) and Pearl Sleet (aka Lawrencium) in operations. Use of PentAGI for WHOIS asset mapping and systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against organizations in Asia. "The emergence of ARTEX and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses," GTIG and Mandiant said. "Frameworks such as ARTEX compress attack timelines to machine speed; however, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces, increasing the likelihood of detection and mitigation."

1809b1v.text: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new Windows infostealer malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER (aka VOLTA) that makes use of a large language model (LLM) to rank a victim's stolen data by their monetization value. Like other typical stealer families, VOLTA is equipped to harvest passwords and cookies from Chromium-based web browsers; data from Outlook profiles and Slack workspaces; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots. "VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine," Cisco Talos researcher Ryan Fetterman said. "This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation." To make this information more valuable, the malware uses stolen session access to search the victim's Gmail account for receipts to corroborate the home address by extracting emails related to Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal. Once the necessary information is collected, the bundle is serialized and fed into an artificial intelligence (AI) system for analysis using OpenRouter, a unified LLM API gateway and routing service, along with a system prompt. The requests are defaulted to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, failing which it falls back to Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash. "VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model's refusal, checking each response for phrases like 'I can't' or 'I'm not able,' before passing on to a chain of up to three models," Talos said. VOLTA features a 240-word system prompt that instructs the model to assume the role of a "forensic intelligence analyst" responsible for drafting a target assessment based on data from a structured evidence bundle. "The bundle is the ONLY permissible source of facts; your training knowledge must never supply a fact about the subject," reads a line from the prompt. "The required output includes a section titled 'WHAT THEY'RE WORTH' with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on 'THEIR OPSEC' containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene," Talos explained. "The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets." Data exfiltration happens over Telegram at three different stages - Right after the stealer runs, containing details about browser passwords, cookies, payment cards, cryptocurrency wallets; Discord, Steam, and Roblox tokens; Wi-Fi passwords, and screenshots After the AI call, which includes the captured data and the results of the LLM analysis After the live enrichment step, which includes Gmail receipts and order histories What's more, VOLTA makes use of a template containing six slots that are filled in at build time. This includes the Telegram channel used for data exfiltration, API keys, and other settings. This approach suggests that the malware author is likely either advertising a builder kit to prospective customers or operating it as a bespoke tool under their control to compile a custom binary for each order. "If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations," Talos said. "It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox." "VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement." The disclosure comes as adversarial adoption of generative AI (aka GenAI) is quickly becoming the new normal, as threat actors incorporate the technology into their workflows to develop custom tools or find valuable data, thereby increasing the likelihood of success of their attacks. "GenAI technologies are also well suited to examine massive amounts of data for the purposes of classification or content searching," Zscaler ThreatLabz said. "Once an attacker has access to the victim’s system, GenAI can therefore be used to search all materials to which a victim's system has access, seeking the most valuable or sensitive data for theft or encryption during the next phase of the attack." A ransomware actor can leverage this method to identify and acquire the most sensitive data from a compromised network, maximizing the chances that the victim will pay up. Last week, Talos also detailed an AI-enabled framework called NIK C2 that gives attackers remote access, credential theft, keylogging, defense evasion, surveillance, and ransomware capabilities, while integrating an OpenAI client to send stolen data for AI analysis within the compromised session. A Go-based, Windows remote access tool, NIK C2 grants persistent control over compromised hosts and supports over 52 commands sent by a command-and-control (C2) server to collect a wide range of data. The OpenAI integration is notable for the fact that the threat actor can abuse a victim's own OpenAI API key to execute the AI-driven analysis. Specifically, the plant checks if the actor has supplied an API key. In the absence of one, it scans the victim's environment variables for the string "OPENAI_API_KEY" and uses it. This is a form of LLMjacking, where bad actors steal access to another party's AI model to run their own operations – in this case, against the victim itself – while the legitimate owner pays for the computing power. In addition, it allows the attacker to evade detection by obscuring who made the requests. "This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications," Talos said. "If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference." "NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows," Talos said.

azxhye.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 01, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security A critical flaw in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud let an attacker log in as a trusted client without holding that client's private key. To do it, the attacker had to reach their HTTPS API over the network and have the trusted client's public certificate. Once in, the attacker would act as that client, with access to the cluster and its virtual machines. If the impersonated account is privileged, the attacker could gain "root access to the host machine," Canonical said. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-112816, carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, and Canonical has released fixed versions of both products. How the Flaw Works LXD and MicroCloud let remote clients access their APIs over mutual TLS, a setup in which the client presents a certificate to prove who it is. A client is trusted when its certificate is in the server's trust store, the list of identities the server will accept. The flaw was in how the server checked that certificate. It compared every certificate the client sent against the trust store, but a TLS connection only proves the client owns the private key for the first certificate in the chain, the leaf. The rest of the chain is whatever the client chose to attach. So an attacker could take a trusted client's public certificate, which is not secret, attach it to the chain behind their own, and the server would accept them as that client. Who Is Affected Using the flaw takes two things: network access to the HTTPS API, and the public certificate of a client the server already trusts. A standalone LXD server does not expose that API by default. It listens only on a local socket unless an administrator turns on the network API with the core.https_address setting. MicroCloud, which ties several machines running LXD into one cluster, has a specific weak point. Canonical said an attacker who can capture a member's public certificate as it joins the cluster can then log in as that member. The CVE record lists LXD 4.0.14, 5.0.10, 5.21.8 and 6.9 as affected, each before the fixed release that follows. Canonical lists these fixed snap versions: Product Snap channel Fixed version LXD 6/stable 6.10.1 LXD 5.21/stable 5.21.9 LXD 5.0/stable 5.0.11 LXD 4.0/stable 4.0.15 MicroCloud 3/stable 3.4.1 MicroCloud 2/stable 2.1.5 The bug did not start at Canonical. The Incus project, which began as a community fork of LXD, reported it, and Canonical confirmed it affected LXD as well. Incus fixed the same flaw in version 7.6.0. Ubuntu's own archive packages of LXD are listed as not affected or not shipped, so the fixed releases are the snaps. There is no public sign the flaw has been used in an attack. The CVE record carries a U.S. CISA assessment, dated October 30, that the flaw is not known to have been exploited; it is not on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and no working exploit has been published. What to Do Update LXD and MicroCloud to the fixed versions. On a snap install, run sudo snap refresh lxd and sudo snap refresh microcloud. Canonical said the fixed LXD point releases were still rolling out from the candidate channel to stable at the time of its advisory, so check the version you actually have after the refresh rather than assume the fix arrived. Canonical's advisory gives no temporary workaround for LXD. Because the attack requires network access to the API, limiting who can reach it reduces risk until you update. The Incus project, reporting the same flaw, said there is no configuration fix and that the only step is to restrict network access to the listener. Incus users should move to 7.6.0, which fixed this flaw along with 17 other security issues.

1r5yhjg.text: Malicious code on the website of prediction market Polymarket sold some signed-in traders' positions and moved their funds to the hackers on October 29. The code had replaced a page-speed script that the site loaded from an outside company. Polymarket says it is refunding about $2.7 million to 726 affected wallets. Blockchain records show crypto worth about $2.64 million reached the hackers' wallet in under an hour. The replaced script came from DebugBear, whose real user monitoring (RUM) tool measures how fast web pages load for real visitors. Researchers at Hudson Rock downloaded the malicious file on October 29 from the address Polymarket's site used to load the DebugBear script. They also found a change in Polymarket's site code that removed the DebugBear script. DebugBear's DNS records were compromised through its domain registrar, the company said on X. Its early findings indicate the attack targeted one customer's website. It has seen no sign of a break-in to its own systems, though it is still looking. Researchers at Ohey found a different server answering for DebugBear's web addresses at 18:13 UTC, when the malicious file was still online. Earlier that day, the normal script had been served from Google Cloud Storage. Each DebugBear customer loads its own copy of the script, and the file that was swapped was Polymarket's. How the Script Took the Money The code reuses the access a signed-in trader already has in an open Polymarket page, Hudson Rock found after reviewing the file without running it. It reads account details that Polymarket keeps in the browser, including a set of trading API keys. Those API keys alone cannot place an order on Polymarket, because orders also need a wallet signature. Hudson Rock found no part of the code that sends the keys, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to the server it reports to. Instead, the code searches the page for the part of Polymarket's site that places orders, and for the signer that approves the account's transactions. It then takes one of two paths. For accounts that sign in with their own crypto wallet, it moves the trader's positions straight to the hackers' wallet. For accounts that sign in via email, it sells positions at ever-worse prices and then moves the money out. In both paths, the code asks the account's own signer to sign its requests and hands them to Polymarket's relayer, which submits them. Hudson Rock said a signing request alone does not prove a trader signed without seeing a prompt. The wallet provider may still ask the trader, refuse, or apply its own rules for the session. The wallet written into the code received its first funds at 17:10 UTC and its last at 18:02 UTC, according to Ohey's blockchain trace. In that time, it collected 28.6 million POL tokens and positions from 33 wallets. At 18:19 UTC, those 28.6 million POL were worth about $2.64 million at DefiLlama's price of $0.0922, DefiPrime calculated. The figure covers only the POL, not the positions. The wallet sent all 28.6 million POL on to three other addresses between 18:28 and 18:38 UTC, its transaction history shows. Polymarket's Response and Refunds Polymarket posted its first status update about unauthorized activity in user wallets at 17:38 UTC. At 18:05 UTC, it said its exchange was in cancel-only mode, with relayer actions paused. The company said it removed the script "within the hour." It also cleared every cache, reset all active login sessions and paused trading until the site was clean. It has referred the case to law enforcement. By October 30, 689 of the 726 affected wallets had been refunded in full, and the remaining 37 were being paid as they were checked. Polymarket is also paying $1.19 million to about 5,500 wallets that lost money during the trading pause or had positions taken. In all, it is returning $3.9 million to traders. Traders do not need to file a claim. Polymarket's status page links a form for anyone who thinks their amount is wrong or that they should have received a payment. What Sites and Traders Can Do DebugBear has told customers of its RUM product to remove its embed code from their websites. The address that served the malicious file, cdn.debugbear[.]com, had no DNS record when The Hacker News checked on November 1.
