Polymarket said it is putting third-party scripts back in place with extra checks, such as a stronger Content Security Policy (CSP), pinned versions, and sandboxing. Hudson Rock's advice for sites that load outside scripts: Keep unneeded third-party code off pages where users trade or sign. Where a file can be pinned, use Subresource Integrity (SRI), which lets the browser reject the file if its contents change. A security policy that simply allows a trusted CDN does not check the files that CDN serves. Check what code on a signed-in page can ask the signer to do. Hudson Rock's advice for traders is to reject any signing request they did not expect.

91ovzm.text: The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets to TraderTraitor, a North Korea-aligned elite hacking group also tracked as Jade Sleet, Pressure Chollima, PUKCHONG, Slow Pisces, and UNC4899. The FBI, along with the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), said it observed the threat actor converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH). "It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages," the FBI said in a statement. The agency has also provided a list of wallet addresses that the attackers are said to be using to launder the stolen assets. The development comes as Binance said it has resumed phase one of withdrawals starting today between 6 and 9 a.m. UTC after they were paused in the wake of the incident. "Since the incident, our teams have taken precautionary measures to safeguard the platform, conducted security assessments, and worked to verify the readiness of affected services," Binance said in a statement. "We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks. Deposit services remain open and are not affected by the incident." The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin. "This single incident almost doubles the total cryptoassets stolen by the regime," blockchain analysis firm Elliptic said. "Actors linked to North Korea, officially the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK), are believed to have stolen over $6.5 billion in cryptoassets in recent years." Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism. TraderTraitor is the name assigned to a North Korean group that has a history of orchestrating cryptocurrency thefts against the Web3.0 industry by tricking victims into downloading malware-laced applications. The cluster is known to be active since at least 2020. In recent years, the adversary has been attributed to cryptocurrency heists targeting DMM Bitcoin, Bybit, KelpDAO, and Bitget. Reports from SentinelOne, Zscaler ThreatLabz, and Microsoft have revealed that TraderTraitor is continuing to hone its tradecraft, using trojanized Terraform providers as a malware distribution vector and leveraging front companies to conduct job-themed targeting against individuals involved in cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, and talent recruitment companies. The poisoned Terraform provider is used to deliver a Bash loader that selects and downloads malware tailored to the victim's operating system. This includes a cross-platform implant called FLATROOF, which siphons sensitive data from the victim using a Python-based information stealer before ultimately dropping the ROOFDECK backdoor to obtain complete remote control. The activity once again demonstrates how North Korean threat actors continue to abuse trusted developer workflows through trojanized Terraform providers to deliver cross-platform malware across macOS, Linux, and Windows systems, and gain persistent access. TraderTraitor's modus operandi, like other North Korea-linked campaigns such as Lazarus Group's Operation Dream Job and Famous Chollima's Contagious Interview, employs recruitment-themed lures as a pretext to convince victims to run malicious code. The social engineering phase is augmented by the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to craft convincing lures, create fake personas, and evade detection. "The actor leveraged tailored domains, social media profiles, and industry-specific knowledge to pose as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company, using software engineer-themed opportunities to initiate contact and schedule interviews with individuals who engaged with the outreach," Microsoft said. "Within this short time frame, Jade Sleet conducted similar job-themed targeting using two additional front companies, supported by comparable infrastructure and relevant domain knowledge."

1ugojcw.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 01, 2026Windows Security / Cyber Espionage Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what has been described as a "highly sophisticated infection chain" targeting government organizations in Asia. The activity, detailed by Kaspersky this week, targeted a custom Windows 10 build used exclusively by government entities in Asia and involves the deployment of a previously undocumented .NET assembly-loading framework codenamed NetamLoader. The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Nor is it clear if the intrusion compromised more than one system and allowed the hackers to steal any sensitive information. The Russian cybersecurity company said the artifact was detected in the first half of 2026, packaged inside a Windows cabinet archive (CAB) file placed in a directory that stores Windows operating system update packages. It's suspected the operation involved a supply chain attack, in which bad actors compromised a trusted third-party vendor to gain access to downstream users who rely on its services or software. The sample in question features a ".config" file that employs AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. AppDomainManager injection is an adversarial technique used to load arbitrary payloads by hijacking .NET Framework's AppDomainManager mechanism when a .NET application starts. Put differently, the approach targets .NET Framework's application-domain initialization to achieve code execution. The end result is the same as DLL sideloading: to run malicious code inside a legitimate application's process so as to fly under the radar. According to Kaspersky, the CAB archive containing the .config file was placed in the path: "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24," with its contents extracted and dropped into "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\." Infection chain: Stage 1 The exact delivery vehicle for the CAB archive remains unknown. Present in the archive are seven files, four of which are legitimate components of Patch My PC, an endpoint management software - fabric.config Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll PatchMyPC-Enum.dll PatchMyPC-Models.dll PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config Resources.resx None of the files with the exception of "Resources.resx" embed malicious code. The infection chain plays out as a two-stage process as follows - The execution of "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe" serves as the launchpad for several payloads. It abuses AppDomainManager injection to parse "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config," resulting in the execution of "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll." Once loaded, "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll" finds "fabric.config" located in the same directory and parses its contents to load "Resources.resx." "Resources.resx" contains "multiple layers" of encoded, compressed, or encrypted payloads, such as XAML files, .NET assemblies, and JSON data, which are decoded and loaded by the component before it. Infection chain: Stage 2 A brief description of these payloads is listed below - XAML-1, a loader for an embedded payload, XAML-2. XAML‑2 initializes the second stage of the attack chain by loading two compressed and Base64‑encoded XAML files: XAML-2-1 and XAML-2-2. XAML-2-1 is used to bypass Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI). XAML-2-2 contains two parts, a .NET module (aka .NET 1 Loader) and a JSON data payload (aka JSON-1). JSON-1, the JSON payload that contains two components: JSON-1-c, which stores command-and-control (C2) server configuration, and JSON-1-p, which contains a Base64‑encoded file (.NET 2 Plugin) and a collection of compressed, encrypted XAML templates used to build XAML-3. XAML-2-2 loads .NET 1 Loader, which then serves as a decrypting, assembling, and loading for XAML‑3, reports the status to the C2 server, and deletes malicious files extracted from the CAB archive, along with CLR usage logs and Windows system Prefetch cache files to cover up the tracks. XAML-3, the XAML payload that runs within "dllhost.exe" and is designed to decode, decompress, and load .NET 2 Plugin. .NET 2 Plugin, a .NET assembly that loads the C2 configuration, gathers system information from Windows Registry, checks if the current host process is "dllhost.exe," waits a random jitter delay of 20-40 minutes before issuing its first request to the C2 server ("openaigpt4v[.]com"), and enters into a periodic polling loop to fetch an XAML file and execute it in an isolated AppDomain. "If a valid response is received from C2, the loop pauses for 5-6 minutes before the next request; otherwise, it pauses for 22-28 hours, checking every 10 minutes to determine whether the allotted time has elapsed," Kaspersky explained. Telemetry data gathered by Kaspersky has identified a single victim in Asia, with NetamLoader designed to attack a Windows 10 build customized for government-only use. Although the targeted Asian country was not disclosed, signs are that it's likely China, as Microsoft offers a bespoke version called Windows 10 China Government Edition specifically for the Chinese government and state-owned entities. Earlier this August, Bloomberg reported that China's Ministry of State Security had ordered some government agencies to stop using the "Government Edition" in favor of Chinese-made Linux distributions as part of an effort to reduce its dependence on foreign technology. "Beijing's instruction stemmed from data security concerns," Bloomberg said, citing "people familiar with the matter." No additional details were disclosed at the time. "In today's geopolitical climate, a growing number of countries are building their own core software platforms, including operating systems, databases, middleware, and cloud services, with operating systems often the top priority," Kaspersky concluded. "The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own. Bringing the operation and maintenance of such a system to maturity is a lengthy process."

blz0sp.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 31, 2026Data Security / Cyber Attack American blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said it was the target of a cybersecurity incident in which an external actor accessed non-sensitive customer data. However, the company noted that the breach did not result in unauthorized access to its investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens. "This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," Chainalysis said Friday. "Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users." The company said it's patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems in response to the incident. The mention of "offensive agentic techniques" indicates that an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tool was used to execute the attack, although Chainalysis offered no details on the specific methods or tactics employed. "We are seeing an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyber attacks, and we are taking a whole-of-company approach to make sure our security posture meets the evolving environment and our customers' expectations," it said. The development comes as adversarial use of AI has ramped up in recent months, with various threat actors using the technology to automate different stages of the attack lifecycle and target hundreds of organizations across multiple industries. This includes a China state-backed threat group known as Vapor Panda, which is using ARTEX, an agentic penetration testing framework, to conduct attacks at scale, compromising about 140 targets in a span of 11 days as part of broad access operation. "AI mainly improves established attacks by making them faster, more personalized, and easier to scale," Abnormal AI said. "Agentic intrusion chains and prompt injection are more distinct because they depend directly on deployed AI systems."

11rij62.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 31, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added two security flaws impacting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following active exploitation in the wild. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-111357 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A missing authentication for a critical function vulnerability that could allow a local authenticated attacker to escalate their privileges. CVE-2026-118527 (CVSS score: 4.3) - A generation of predictable numbers or identifiers vulnerability that could allow a remote authenticated attacker to upload files with attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk. It's worth noting that the security bugs are part of an exploit chain that was first documented by Volexity earlier this month as weaponized in conjunction with an authentication bypass flaw (CVE-2026-104935, CVSS score: 8.6) by a previously undocumented threat actor dubbed UTA0576. CVE-2026-104935 was added to the KEV catalog on October 13, 2026. "This exploit chain combined an authentication bypass, a remote code execution (RCE), and a privilege escalation vulnerability to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution," Volexity noted. Unlike other attacks that typically exploit such flaws to deploy web shells or malware, UTA0576 has been observed leveraging the flaws to extract credentials and limited Active Directory metadata; conduct host reconnaissance; and search for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. Ivanti said that, around the time the details were published, it was still working on developing fixes for the local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerability exploited in the attack chain. Patches for both CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 are now available in the following versions of ICS - 25.1.1.2 and prior (Fixed in 25.1.1.3) 22.8R2.5 and prior (Fixed in 22.8R2.6) "At the time of discovery of exploitation, Ivanti had a fix developed for CVE-2026-104935 which was already in QA for supported versions, and we made the decision to not delay getting a fix to customers that resolved the primary exploitation path when the LPE was discovered," Ivanti explained. "Because of this, our focus was initially centered on the disclosure of CVE-2026-104935 and providing protection for our customers as quickly as possible." The company also noted that it discovered a portion of this vulnerability as part of its product security program and patched it in the July release 25.1.3.0, adding it had been working to backport the fix to other supported versions when exploitation activity occurred. The latest release addresses all vulnerabilities which were chained and exploited in the wild. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are required to apply the fixes for CVE-2026-111357 by November 2, 2026, and CVE-2026-118527 by November 13, 2026.

gukvs2.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 31, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security A malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, allowing them to read their private conversations, researchers at the security firm Parameter showed. The researchers reported the flaw through OpenAI's bug bounty program on October 18, and OpenAI fixed it eight days later and rated it P1, its most serious category. The trap was an ordinary ChatGPT conversation shared via its public link. It could be sent the same way as any real shared chat: by email, as a chat message, as a support ticket, or as a social post. The victim did not have to install anything, join a workspace, or sign in through the attacker. In the most reliable version of the attack, they opened the link and clicked ChatGPT's Preview button once. In a later version, Parameter set the page to open Preview on its own, so opening the link was the only step. What the Attacker Could Do Once the link opened, the attacker's code ran inside the victim's signed-in session with the same access as the real ChatGPT site. It listed the victim's recent conversations, opened a private chat that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent a small portion of it to a server controlled by the researchers. The code called ChatGPT's own signed-in APIs directly, rather than copying what happened to be on the screen. Because it ran with the victim's full web access, its reach was not limited to those chats. "Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account," the researchers wrote. The work was a controlled test. Parameter does not report any real-world use of the flaw, and ran its private-chat proof between separate accounts rather than against real users. How the Link Broke Out of Its Sandbox Here is how the chain worked, according to Parameter. ChatGPT can turn a block of HTML in a chat into a small web page through a feature called Preview. Because that page can hold any code, ChatGPT runs it in a locked-down frame on a separate web address, where it cannot read the main ChatGPT page around it. That sandbox held. The way in came from a second feature in the same conversation. The shared chat also contained an interactive graph, and drawing it loaded a math library called MathLive into the main ChatGPT page. Loading MathLive left a listener running there that accepted messages about its on-screen keyboard. A message passed between browser frames is safe only if the receiver checks who sent it. Parameter found that this listener accepted a keyboard message from any sender, and that the message was allowed to carry raw HTML. The Preview could then reach across the boundary and hand attacker HTML to the trusted main page. That HTML built a new frame that the browser treated as part of chatgpt.com. A script loaded from YouTube then supplied the code that ran inside it. ChatGPT's content security policy limits where a page's scripts may come from. It blocked inline code but allowed scripts from YouTube, which is why that step worked. What OpenAI Fixed, and What Users Should Do Parameter said OpenAI reproduced both the code execution and the private-chat proof, raised the severity from P2 to P1, and rolled a fix across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. By October 26, both versions rejected the messages the attack relied on. The researchers traced the problem to three design choices that lined up: MathLive acted on a message that changed its settings without checking which frame had sent it. That message was allowed to carry raw HTML as keyboard-layout data. The HTML could create a frame that was not sandboxed and inherited the chatgpt.com identity. The YouTube step was only the final workaround, not the cause. Blocking it alone would still leave an untrusted Preview able to push HTML into the main site. ChatGPT users do not need to do anything. The fix is on OpenAI's side, with nothing to install or reset. Parameter published its writeup on October 28, after the fix. OpenAI paid a total of $5,000 for the report.

vvgq5d.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 31, 2026Threat Intelligence / Network Security Threat actors are launching about 8,226 network-layer distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks per hour, Cloudflare revealed Thursday. The web infrastructure and security company said it autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer (L3) DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests in the third quarter of 2026. That amounts to 197,400 attacks per day, or one attack every 0.44 seconds. In comparison, a total of 13.2 million and 10.0 million L3 DDoS attacks were recorded in Q2 and Q1 2026, respectively. The increase has been linked to DDoS-for-hire booter or stresser services that are responsible for hundreds of thousands of attacks. "Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%," the Cloudforce One threat intelligence team said in its quarterly DDoS Threat Report shared with The Hacker News. An interesting trend is the decline of hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps by 69% from the previous quarter – going from 805 attacks in Q2 to 251 in Q3 – likely as a result of law enforcement actions against AISURU, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad earlier this March. Still, the threat remains far from completely neutralized, given the emergence of new variants like Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot, Cloudflare warned. Another notable shift is the decline in Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CLDAP) floods, while DNS amplification jumped 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks. The most targeted industries include media, production, and publishing; information technology and services; gambling and casinos; computer software; and telecommunications providers. The U.S., China, Indonesia, the U.K., and Türkiye emerged as the most attacked countries during the time period, with Canada and Israel entering the top 10 ranking, fueled by attacks targeting Canada's retail, telecommunications, and marketing sectors.

1vp329y.text: Chinese state-sponsored threat actors have been observed using a Go-based artificial intelligence (AI)-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX in attacks aimed at high-value targets simultaneously. The activity has been attributed by CrowdStrike to a China-based "targeted intrusion adversary" it tracks under the moniker Vapor Panda (previously VexatiousTemper). First identified in February 2021, the hacking group overlaps with a threat cluster detailed by Trend Micro as Earth Estries. "Agentic tooling like ARTEX enables this scale of expansion at speed, allowing a small team to pursue a wider target set than manual operations would support, rather than a wholesale shift away from the adversary's established access-development mission," CrowdStrike said in a Thursday analysis. Starting October 17, 2026, Vapor Panda is said to have used the AI tool against more than 200 distinct organizations across the world, including foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; semiconductor, defense, and think tank organizations in the U.S.; and telecommunications providers in multiple regions. Some of the notable targets listed by CrowdStrike are listed below - Foreign ministries of two Latin America-based countries, Central America, and Asia A Middle East-based interior ministry A European country's foreign ministry, presidency, and prime minister's office, along with defense, justice, finance, and intelligence entities 19 U.S.-based organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors Telecommunications providers in the U.S., Belgium, and the Philippines Post-exploitation activity has been confirmed at nine organizations, allowing the attacker to deploy BLOODALCHEMY, a derivative of ShadowPad, followed by credential spraying, network scanning, and reconnaissance. Vapor Panda is also said to have conducted password-spraying and credential-scanning activity against at least 12 additional organizations, including U.S.-based think tanks and government entities in Europe. Central to the operation is the use of ARTEX with DeepSeek and an as-yet-unknown, subscription-based commercial large language model (LLM) to conduct the intrusions at scale, leveraging an army of planner and worker agents that coordinate with each other in pursuit of a common goal to move from initial access to host reconnaissance and lateral movement. A human operator in the loop oversees the operation, directing the agents to write web shells, extract domain administrator passwords, and enumerate endpoint sensor coverage. "In a single intrusion, Vapor Panda's planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens, indicating the scale of the automated activity and implying far higher consumption across the operation as a whole," CrowdStrike said. Unlike some campaigns that used to assist with individual digital break-ins, the use of ARTEX is at a much higher level to run multiple engagements concurrently, with the human operator only stepping in to steer the agents to accomplish their objective, while taking steps to bypass endpoint defenses. Analysis of the recovered transcripts highlights the use of ARTEX in combination with tried-and-tested approaches - Chaining an unsigned Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion and an XML external entity (XXE) flaw to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service. This is followed by obtaining a role that can issue administration commands to thousands of instances before escalating access to recover an enterprise administrator account. Deploying web shells, abusing an unauthenticated orchestration service to obtain root access in a production container environment, reading Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords, and leveraging resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account. Supplying the agent with a set of authentication keys that had not been rotated since 2022, which then uses those keys to forge an administrator token and read mailboxes. In the next phase, the agent uses VPN configurations recovered from a user's sent mail, along with a VPN client key originating from a purported May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network. "Across these engagements, the agents pursued multiple attack paths in parallel, spanning web applications, cloud services, container environments, Active Directory, and mail and VPN infrastructure," CrowdStrike explained. "They shifted to alternative approaches when a path failed. This breadth likely enables a single operator to apply a wider range of techniques against more targets at once than would be feasible through manual operations." The development comes as ARTEX has witnessed broad adoption among threat actors in a short span of time, prompting its developer Li Puhua ("Autumn-27") to take it closed source. "It orchestrates multiple LLM backends to autonomously perform reconnaissance, vulnerability identification, and exploitation, significantly lowering the technical barrier for conducting complex intrusion campaigns," Zscaler ThreatLabz said in a report published earlier this month. One of Many Panda Threat Clusters The disclosure also coincides with the emergence of four previously undocumented China-linked state-sponsored threat groups known as Hollow Panda, Overcast Panda, Titan Panda, and Veiled Panda, which have targeted a broad range of sectors across the world for intelligence gathering and intellectual property theft. Overcast Panda, described as "one of the most operationally sophisticated and persistent threats facing organizations with personnel traveling to China," has been linked to close access intrusions in which the adversary has deployed their proprietary FlowCloud backdoor on victims' devices via direct physical access when those targets were in the country. FlowCloud is launched by means of DLL sideloading, with its components designed to fly under the radar and resist forensic analysis. Command-and-control (C2) is accomplished through legitimate cloud infrastructure in an attempt to further conceal their presence. "FlowCloud itself is a sophisticated, purpose-built tool uniquely associated with Overcast Panda," CrowdStrike said. "Once deployed, FlowCloud provides the adversary with persistent, covert remote access to the target device, enabling keylogging, screen capture, file collection, and credential harvesting." Titan Panda, on the other hand, has been observed targeting legal billing software by exploiting a hard-coded Internet Information Services (IIS) machine key vulnerability in Intapp Time Server to achieve remote code execution across law firms. The attacks, first detected in April 2026, led to the deployment of an in-memory framework called IceGiant to carry out reconnaissance, persistence, lateral movement, and data exfiltration. The threat actor is assessed to be operational since at least 2021, compromising several legal organizations in North America for over two years. "How Titan Panda obtained the default machine keys is unknown, though IIS compromise of a legal entity running Intapp Time Server may have exposed the hardcoded keys in the application's configuration file, enabling ViewState deserialization attacks against any organization running default installations," CrowdStrike said.

flr5.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 30, 2026Vulnerability / Endpoint Security TeamViewer has fixed a flaw that lets the machine being controlled in a remote session attack the computer that connected to control it. In a TeamViewer session, the computer that connects and takes control is the viewer, and the machine it controls is the host. A malicious or compromised host can exploit the flaw to crash the viewer's TeamViewer and, depending on the platform, may also run code on the viewer's computer. This works only after the user starts a remote-control session to that host. The fix is in TeamViewer version 15.83. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-111585 and scored 8.8 out of 10, in the high range. It affects the TeamViewer Full Client on Windows, Linux, and macOS, the Windows Portable edition, and the Android Remote Control app, in all versions before 15.83. For this flaw, TeamViewer's bulletin lists the Full Client, Portable, and Android app, but not the Host. The same 15.83 update fixes two other flaws in that bulletin that do affect the Host, so people running the Host should update as well. Omri Dar, a researcher at security firm Remedio, published a technical account of the flaw on October 29. In this bug, he wrote, "the attacker is the host and the victim is the viewer." In a remote session, the host tells the viewer how large its screen image is. The viewer uses that size to set aside memory, but the calculation can overflow and reserve too little. Screen data that arrives afterward is then written past the end of that space. At a minimum, this crashes the viewer's TeamViewer session, and the host can trigger the crash again whenever they want. On Windows, Remedio says it took the bug further, bypassing the operating system's built-in exploit defenses and running code of its choosing in the viewer. The demonstration used a stand-in on the host to supply part of the attack data, so it is not yet an attack carried out entirely over the network. That result was shown only on Windows. Whether the same works on macOS, Linux, or Android is not covered in the write-up. TeamViewer only says that code execution is possible, depending on the platform. The attack needs no password and no extra click beyond accepting the session, and it works in TeamViewer's default setup, Dar wrote. The flaw affects all versions before 15.83, including 15.82, the security update TeamViewer released in September. Updating last month did not remove it. What to Do The only fix TeamViewer offers is to update, and it lists no workaround. Current users should move to 15.83 or later. The fixed builds for older supported branches are in the table above. The same 15.83 update also fixes two other high-severity flaws in the same bulletin, including a separate code-execution flaw affecting Linux and macOS. A companion bulletin the same day, TV-2026-1012, fixes six more flaws in TeamViewer's Remote Management add-ons, delivered by automatic update. TeamViewer said that when it published the fix, it was unaware of any attacks exploiting the flaw. The vulnerability is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of its October 29 listing. Remedio reported no attacks in the wild and did not release exploit code.

1u3520n.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit a high-severity security flaw in WordPress Core shortly after patches were released. The vulnerability, which does not have a CVE identifier, relates to a case of remote code execution impacting WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3. It carries a CVSS score of 8.1 on the CVSS scoring system. Patches for the flaw were released on October 28, 2026. "This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades," Wordfence said. "This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window." The WordPress security company noted that successful exploitation requires an "attacker to hit a very narrow window while WordPress is unpacking a complete Core update." The issue boils down to the fact that affected versions unpack new files part of a full-package Core update into a predictable directory under "wp-content/upgrade." This copy also includes the WordPress installer. "Because the staging directory is web-accessible on many servers, an unauthenticated attacker who requests the installer at precisely the right moment can interact with the staged WordPress copy and progress to PHP code execution," Alex Thomas, who leads the Wordfence Threat Response Team, said. A threat actor who is able to win the race condition can gain the ability to execute code on the server, assuming the following conditions are met - A full-package update containing the installer files Public web and PHP access to the staging tree A predictable or discovered staging path, and Adequate time to complete the attack before WordPress cleans up the temporary files Although that window has been observed to last only seconds in normal lab environments, threat actors are polling vulnerable paths, such as "setup-config.php," repeatedly in an attempt to trigger the flaw. Over the past 24 hours, Wordfence said it has blocked 62,969 attacks targeting the vulnerability. "Two of the largest sources repeatedly polled small groups of sites for roughly 14.5 hours, behavior consistent with trying to catch the brief upgrade window," Thomas said. "Other sources tested many staging-directory and version-name variations." "Not every request used the exact vulnerable path, but the sustained polling and exact-layout probes show that attackers quickly understood the race condition and began targeting it." With active exploitation attempts already underway, WordPress site owners are advised to update to version 7.1.4 as soon as possible and look for suspicious requests to PHP files located under "wp-content/upgrade," as well as unfamiliar administrator accounts, plugins, or PHP files.

16y8qfw.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Hardware Security / Cryptocurrency A Trezor Safe 5 hardware wallet bought from the reseller CryptoBilis has an extra circuit board that sends out the recovery phrase over a mobile network, a customer has reported. Trezor has not yet examined the device. It is telling everyone who bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March 2026 to move their funds to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase. Trezor said in a blog post on October 30 that the report came in two days earlier from a customer in Indonesia. He bought the wallet from CryptoBilis in August, through the marketplace Tokopedia. The board sits between the wallet's main board and its screen, with a cellular module and an antenna, according to the report. It reads the screen, including the recovery phrase (Trezor calls it the wallet backup), and sends it out whenever the device is plugged in. Trezor has the customer's photos and description and has interviewed him on a video call. It is arranging for the wallet to be sent to its lab. Trezor finds the report believable enough to warn buyers now. "Waiting for lab confirmation would leave CryptoBilis buyers exposed in the meantime," the company said. No CryptoBilis buyer has reported losing funds to Trezor, which cannot see what customers hold in their wallets. The customer had moved his funds off the wallet before he found the board. Trezor's advice covers every Trezor model bought from CryptoBilis since March 2026, from any store that sold devices CryptoBilis supplied, including its store on Tokopedia: If you already use the wallet, move your funds to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase as soon as possible. Restoring the old recovery phrase on another device does not help, because a tampered wallet could already have sent that phrase out. If you have no other secure hardware wallet, move the funds for now to a software wallet or an exchange you know. If you have not set up the wallet, do not set it up, and never type your existing recovery phrase into it. Keep the CryptoBilis device and contact Trezor Support. Trezor will ship you a new device or give you a voucher that covers the cost of one. If you are not sure where your device came from, check the seller's name on your receipt or contact Trezor Support. As of October 30, Trezor had no reports involving any other reseller. Owners cannot reliably check a device themselves and should not weigh or open it to try it, according to Trezor. The customer noticed a weight difference, but small differences can have other causes. Trezor also expects scammers to use the incident to carry out phishing through fake emails, letters, and phone calls. Trezor dropped CryptoBilis, its authorized reseller in Southeast Asia, on October 9, after hardware wallet maker Ledger began investigating losses among Ledger customers who had bought from CryptoBilis. Ledger has since said that one affected customer's wallet contained an unauthorized hardware implant built to capture the recovery phrase during setup. Trezor says the board reported in its Safe 5 appears to work like the implants seen in Ledger devices. Trezor will not compare the two while investigations continue, because each maker builds its devices differently. It does not know who is responsible. Separate Police Advisory in Singapore The Singapore Police Force said in an advisory on October 28 that Ledger hardware wallets bought from some retail stores in Singapore contained malicious hardware components. At least two cases have been reported since September 10. The components could capture users' recovery phrases or private keys. Police investigations are ongoing, and Ledger is reviewing the affected cases.

u1dfjn.text: The alert is critical. The fix is known. And the ticket sits in a queue for days. Security teams understand the risk, but the people who keep applications available need proof that the change won’t break anything. Their concerns are practical. An IPS protection could block legitimate traffic. A configuration change could interrupt a service. An endpoint policy could affect an application the business depends on. Without evidence, the recommendation waits. Safe remediation answers that hesitation with evidence. It tests the proposed action against your environment, applies the approved change, and confirms the result. Security and operations teams decide together, with facts. The Cost of Leaving Protection in Detect Many organizations already own protection they don’t enforce. Signatures sit inactive or in Detect mode while teams weigh false positives, inspection capacity, and business continuity. Meanwhile, applications and traffic patterns change, exceptions pile up, and policies drift away from how the environment runs today. In the Safe Remediation white paper, 47% of the organizations measured had less than 50% protection enablement. Much of the capability they need is already in their environments. Turning everything on isn’t the answer. Every activation carries risk. Teams need to know which changes matter for a given exposure, and how each will behave in production today. Figure 1. Operational pressures and configuration drift can delay enforcement. Build Confidence Before Enforcement Safe remediation follows four stages: Observe, Prove, Act, and Confirm. Evidence carries the proposed response through each stage, with review and approval where required. Observation starts with data your security and IT systems already produce. Vulnerability findings, IPS traffic, device utilization, endpoint policies, and configuration states show what surrounds the proposed change. Then comes proof, and the method fits the technology. An IPS protection can inspect production traffic in Detect mode, giving teams evidence about false positives and performance before it progresses to Prevent. Operating system hardening can use a selected test group, with each host rechecked after execution. Endpoint settings can be assessed against the vendor's hardening baseline. The decision becomes specific to your environment. Security teams explain the protection they expect. Infrastructure and application owners judge the effect on the systems they run. Figure 2. Validation connects environmental evidence with approval, execution, and confirmation. Use Existing Controls While Waiting For a Permanent Fix Patching remains essential for addressing the underlying vulnerability. Testing, coordination, and deployment schedules can extend the time before a patch reaches production, creating a period when additional protection may be needed. An existing IPS signature or virtual patch can help block the relevant exploit path during that period. Correlating vulnerability data with control coverage shows whether a suitable protection exists and whether it is inactive, in Detect mode, or already enforced. That context helps teams select the response. A protection awaiting enforcement may be a candidate for validation and activation. An exposure without a compensating control may require urgent patching or another action. The remediation record should distinguish interim protection from a permanent fix. A compensating control can reduce immediate exposure while the underlying vulnerability remains open and requires follow through. Keep Approval and Execution Connected Once an action has been evaluated, organizations can require approval of its scope or permit automated execution through configured workflows. The approved change then runs through the system responsible for the affected control. IPS changes can use the security management server, operating system hardening can use existing patch management infrastructure, and supported endpoint changes can use the vendor API. This approach lets teams work through the technologies already deployed. Confirmation completes the process. Policy installation can establish that an IPS protection reached enforcement. Host checks can verify a hardening change. Execution records can show failed or pending actions that still need attention, alongside the user, timestamp, and associated exposure. Measure the Protection That Follows Success should include evidence that the intended protection is active after execution. Subsequent security events can show whether a newly enabled control blocked activity associated with the exposure. Across the measured organizations, remediation actions recorded a 99.5% success rate. Over one month, protections applied through remediation subsequently blocked 703.56 million attacks, including 21 million within 24 hours of remediation. These results describe the analyzed environments and provide evidence of protection following enforcement. Figure 3. Remediation outcomes across the environments measured in the white paper. Make Safe Remediation Part of Exposure Management Prioritization establishes where action should begin. Safe remediation gives teams a controlled path for carrying that decision into production, with evidence supporting the proposed change and confirmation showing its result. Check Point Exposure Management connects exposure prioritization with environmental validation, controlled execution, and confirmation through existing security technologies. Security teams can use that process to reduce exposure while evaluating the operational impact of each response. Download Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production to explore the framework, validation methods, and measured outcomes behind this approach.

1p9q35w.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 30, 2026Cyber Crime / Cyber Espionage Ahmad Umar Agha, a Syrian Electronic Army hacker known online as "Th3Pr0," has been sentenced by a U.S. federal court to 42 months in prison for his role in a hacking conspiracy that targeted Western news outlets. The conspiracy was organized and led by members of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's inner circle, including the commander of Syria's General Intelligence Directorate, the U.S. Justice Department said on October 29. The pro-Assad Syrian Electronic Army began its attacks in 2011. Its members sent phishing emails to steal employees' passwords, then used those passwords to deface websites, redirect web traffic, and hijack social media accounts, according to a 2014 FBI affidavit. On April 23, 2013, the group hijacked the Associated Press's Twitter account and posted a false report that President Barack Obama had been injured in two explosions at the White House. Twitter's message confirming a password reset for that account was sent to a Gmail account used primarily by Agha, the affidavit says. The Justice Department said Agha carried out that hack, which caused a temporary $136 billion drop in the value of stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Agha later told Business Insider that a big drop in the Dow "was our goal of that hack attack" and that "it was a big victory for us." Agha was first charged in June 2014 in a complaint that remained secret until March 2016. That month, the FBI added him and co-defendant Firas Dardar to its Cyber's Most Wanted list with a $100,000 reward. A federal grand jury indicted both men in May 2018. Court Watch reported in December 2025 that Agha was in U.S. custody and had appeared in federal court the month before. Three earlier public documents in the case do not describe Syrian officials organizing or leading the group: the 2014 FBI affidavit, the Justice Department's March 2016 announcement of the charges, and its May 2018 announcement of the indictment. In the 2016 announcement, the department said the group acted "in support of" the Syrian government. An early study of the group, published by the OpenNet Initiative, found no credible evidence directly linking the attackers to the Syrian government beyond the unspoken support any such group would need to operate on Syrian networks. In announcing the sentence, the department also said the conspiracy collected intelligence for Assad's government, which fell in December 2024. "Agha deployed his hacking skills in the service of Assad's regime to silence reporting on the regime's atrocities, intimidate its opponents, and incite U.S. servicemembers to refuse their orders," said John A. Eisenberg, Assistant Attorney General for National Security. In all, Agha hacked about 47 Western media outlets, businesses, non-profit groups, and U.S. and allied government bodies, the department said. He got into the company that hosted the U.S. Marine Corps recruiting website and redirected its visitors to an image urging Marines to refuse their orders and fight alongside the Syrian Army. About 3,500 potential visitors saw that image instead of recruiting material. He also twice tried to take over the White House's social media accounts by stealing White House staff email passwords. Once, he got into staff email but failed to trick other staff into giving him access. The FBI affidavit describes the group breaking into a White House staff member's personal email account in July 2013 and says no official White House account was compromised. Many victims spent large sums on cleanup and security upgrades, according to court filings cited by the department. One company that supplies online publishers with content, ads, and links lost about $35,000 a day for about six months. A global non-profit group lost $480,000, including about $250,000 on new network monitoring tools, and had to retrain more than 800 staff members. Dardar remains a fugitive, the department said. He was also charged in a separate case with Peter Romar, a Syrian national then living in Germany. Romar was extradited to the U.S. and pleaded guilty in 2016.

1ndcl3g.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed that a trojanized version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through the Cursor Marketplace as a legitimate update, attempting to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems. The malicious update, version 2.1.313, was distributed under the extension's legitimate publisher identity, prompting Cursor to temporarily shut down its marketplace to remove the compromised package. The exact method attackers used to introduce the unauthorized update remains unclear. "We identified a security incident affecting a modified Claude Code VS Code extension accessed through our Cursor IDE extension marketplace, impacting at most 5,000 users," Cursor said. "This malicious version of the extension was not developed by Anthropic. It does not impact other extensions downloaded from the cursor[.]com/marketplace, Grok Bot, Grok, or our other SpaceXSI product. However, Cursor's statement that the malicious version "was not developed by Anthropic" misses the point. The attackers distributed it as version 2.1.313 under Anthropic's legitimate Claude Code extension ID (anthropic.claude-code), rather than as a separate fake extension. "The package identifies itself as anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313, but its main JavaScript bundle contains a malicious 66-line loader inserted before the legitimate extension code," Jenn Gile, co-founder of OpenSourceMalware, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. The malicious update was distributed only through Cursor's marketplace, with no evidence that it reached Open VSX or Microsoft's official VS Code Marketplace. Users who installed Claude Code through either of those marketplaces are not known to be affected by this incident. As of October 30, 2026, the malicious version has been removed, and Anthropic has published version 2.1.314 to both Open VSX and Microsoft VS Code Marketplace. The extension is designed to activate after VS Code startup and when its webview opens, then proceeds to add an attacker-controlled key to the user's "~/.ssh/authorized_keys" file. The key is labeled "svc-telemetry" in an attempt to make it appear harmless. Subsequently, it attempts to make the victim reachable through SSH across Windows, Linux, and macOS, establishes a reverse tunnel to "134.209.82[.]225," installs platform-specific persistence in the form of a scheduled task, crontab, and LaunchAgent, and transmits host reconnaissance data to "134.209.82[.]225:8099/beacon" on port 8099 over an unencrypted HTTP request. "Turning on the local SSH service requires admin rights, which the malicious extension does not have on most macOS and Windows hosts," the SpaceXAI-owned company said in its own analysis of the incident. "On those hosts the step fails and the attacker could not have logged in through the tunnel. The extension still adds the attacker's SSH key, installs persistence, and sends host details to the attacker. Follow the remediation steps below regardless." The collected data includes - Public IP address from api.ipify[.]org Hostname and local username Operating system and CPU architecture Home directory and current working directory Global Git email from git config --global user.email Names of up to 40 environment variables containing KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP "Environment-variable values are not placed directly in the initial beacon," security researcher Paul McCarty said. "Their names can still reveal which cloud providers, CI systems, and credential types are configured. More importantly, successful SSH access would allow the operator to inspect the account directly." No other follow-on payloads have been observed. That said, the establishment of a reverse tunnel provides a pathway to the victim's SSH service, allowing the operator to issue commands or transfer files. "It was pulled very quickly, but anyone who has their Claude Code instance set to auto-update could have consumed the malware," Gile said. Cursor has revealed that the incident has affected at most 5,000 users who installed the malicious version between about 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. PT on October 29, 2026. The company also said that it will be reaching out to impacted users directly. Users who have installed the compromised extension during the window are advised to isolate the hosts, remove the unauthorized SSH key and persistence mechanisms, and rotate credentials and sessions. The disclosure comes a little over a week after an unknown attacker replaced the release binaries of five already-published versions of OVHcloud's official CLI ("ovh/ovhcloud-cli") with a secret-stealing malware after uploading them through a GitHub account of a legitimate OVH contributor ("HassenBF") hijacked in March 2026 as part of the GlassWorm operation. (An earlier version of the story stated that the extension on the Open VSX registry was compromised. The incident has since been traced back to a compromise of the Cursor VS Code Marketplace.)

1jq8q8n.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Drupal has warned that threat actors are exploiting a "highly critical" security flaw in its Commerce Core component. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-118539 (CVSS score: N/A), is a case of missing authorization affecting Commerce Core versions from 0.0.0 to 2.41 and from 3.0.0 to 3.3.13. "This module enables you to sell goods and services to customers through an included shopping cart and checkout form or through decoupled applications via APIs," Drupal said in an advisory. "The module doesn't sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor." The open-source content-management framework acknowledged that the vulnerability is being "actively exploited in the wild," but provided no specifics about the nature of the activity or the extent of the campaign. Users are being recommended to update to the latest version - Version 3.x - Upgrade to Commerce Core 3.3.13 Earlier versions - Upgrade to Commerce Core 8.x-2.41 Drupal has credited researchers Dan Puccetti (dpuccetti), Marcus Johansson (marcus_johansson), and Robert Snyder (rsnyd) with reporting the flaw. The development comes as two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2), and collectively referred to as PHP2Shell, are witnessing active exploitation attempts in the wild. As of October 25, the percentage of organizations significantly affected by PHP2Shell has declined to 52.1%, according to data from Google-owned Wiz. The cloud security company said it has so far observed two types of activities, including attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism that match public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. The other category refers to "PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities that instead relied on session poisoning and a separate local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability in the application," Wiz researchers Yaara Shriki, Shahar Dorfman, Alma Blachsan, and Yaron Samuel said. "Our observations show that triggering memory exhaustion alone is not enough to complete the exploit chain. Differences in PHP builds, memory limits and worker behavior can prevent subsequent stages from working. The challenge for opportunistic attackers is turning currently available public PoCs into similarly reliable operational tooling or developing it on their own."

qtut4t.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Vulnerability / DevSecOps The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Thursday added two security flaws impacting Cisco and GitLab software to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS score: 10.0) - An integer overflow or wraparound vulnerability in GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition that could allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration due to insufficient regular expression validation. CVE-2026-76418 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An unchecked return value to NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition. The development comes after Cisco said it became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability earlier this month. It has not publicly identified the attackers, the number of targeted organizations, or the actions taken by attackers after gaining initial access. As for CVE-2026-97229, its addition relates to a security incident disclosed by Alpine Linux in which an unknown threat actor unsuccessfully attempted to exploit the flaw targeting its instance on October 20 and 21, 2026. Specifically, the attacker probed an unpatched GitLab instance by sending crafted CI configurations, causing the GitLab worker processes to crash eight times. In four of those crashes, the exploit failed at the next step. The threat actor also downloaded Alpine Linux's GitLab container image. Subsequent attempts by the attacker to get back in on October 25 and 26 were blocked. "The attack came close to working," the maintainers of the security-focused Linux distribution said. "We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with." In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 1, 2026.

xhqa1i.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Cyber Attack / Cryptocurrency Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that a "security incident" on its platform has impacted about $6.3 billion worth of assets. The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said nearly $3 billion of those assets have been frozen on-chain so far. Tether and Circle said they have frozen more than 1.567 billion USDT and 800 million USDT related to the incident, respectively. The Arbitrum Security Council is said to have executed a transaction to freeze about $30.5 million from the Binance Exploit. "Initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," Binance said in an update. The company said there is no evidence of a wallet private key leak, adding it will cover all losses from the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) fund and its own funds. Out of an abundance of caution, Binance has also taken the following steps - Temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed Revoked the affected address authorization; Engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice," Binance said. In an update, Binance said it expects withdrawals to resume in 48 hours, after its team "completes a security revamp of the withdrawal service and its related addresses." The development makes it the biggest cryptocurrency heist recorded to date, surpassing the theft of about $1.5 billion from Bybit in February 2025. The incident was subsequently attributed to North Korea. "Our current estimate on the amount stolen is approximately $5.912 billion at time of theft, nearly 4x the amount stolen in the next largest crypto heist," blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis said in an X post. Attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor TRM Labs has attributed the record-breaking hack targeting Binance to threat actors from North Korea with high confidence. The blockchain analytics company attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which was also behind the 2025 Bybit heist. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," TRM Labs said. "The laundering observed so far, built on large swaps through market makers and lending protocols, differs from the bridge-heavy pattern that followed Bybit." TRM Labs said preparation for the attack was underway at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers taking over a Binance hot wallet to send its "entire balance to an attacker-controlled address" - At 20:20 UTC, the operator submitted a single transaction containing 50 authorizations. Each was signed by the Binance hot wallet, and each pointed it to a sweeper contract that accepts instructions only from the operator. Every wallet keeps a running count of its transactions, called a nonce, and an authorization works only at the count the wallet has reached at the moment it executes. The Binance hot wallet processes a steady flow of withdrawals, so its count keeps moving forward. By preparing signatures for 50 consecutive counts, the attacker guaranteed that one would still be valid when the transaction executed. One matched, which was all the attacker needed. The signatures were produced in advance as a batch. Three minutes and 24 seconds after the delegation, the operator instructed the Binance hot wallet to send its entire balance to an attacker-controlled address. That single transaction moved 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including 1.615 billion USDT. The most likely explanation is that the attacker gained the ability to make Binance's hot wallet signing system sign transactions of its choosing across chains. The batch of 50 pre-signed authorizations suggests the access may have been limited in time, or that signatures had to be requested through a system. Binance has yet to publish a root cause. So far, Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial have frozen about $2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council has frozen about $30 million in ETH and ARB. The attacker continues to retain control of more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth about $2.4 billion, plus smaller amounts on other chains.

1vjops2.text: Some attacks take real skill. Others just need someone to leave a door open. This week has both. Exposed passwords, old bugs still getting exploited, and trusted software doing things it shouldn't.There's a strange mix of clever tricks and careless mistakes. Hackers are borrowing trust from familiar apps, websites, and AI tools. Some are using AI to speed things up. Others are leaving their own attack files exposed. Not exactly careful work.Different stories, familiar weak spots. Here's what showed up this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. PHP2Shell attacks persist WordPress security company Wordefence said it's not aware of any WordPress site compromised through PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) as of October 28, 2026. "We continue to see PHP2Shell-related requests across the more than 5 million sites we protect," it said. "Those requests show ongoing scanning and exploitation attempts; they do not show whether an attempt succeeded. Our site-cleaning and incident response teams have not handled a WordPress compromise attributed to these vulnerabilities." 40,573 secrets exposed Hudson Rock's investigation into the FortiBleed credential harvesting campaign has uncovered 975 newly identified domains and 40,573 exposed secrets, including 37,076 local-user records and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records. The data comes from newly obtained 1,703 FortiGate source files associated with 1,689 host identifiers. "The configuration material dates to around February 2026, earlier than the likely May/June material examined in the first investigation," Hudson Rock said. The latest discovery has been codenamed FortiBleed 2.0. Institutional DNS hijacked Threat actors have used domain shadowing to place illegal gambling content beneath legitimate school and government domains in two unrelated operations. "In both cases, an unauthorized party appears to have gained access to DNS administration and created records that the original domain owners may not have noticed," Infoblox said. "Because the resulting hostnames sat within established institutional namespaces, they provided especially useful infrastructure for search-engine optimization (SEO) and traffic acquisition." One cluster, linked to a threat actor called Hidden Hawk, has been found to add individual CNAME records that mapped institutional hostnames to gambling pages hosted largely on Cloudflare Pages. The second campaign exploiting an Indian government domain "delegated entire subzones to third-party authoritative nameservers and used a wildcard, allowing many hostnames to be managed outside the victim's DNS environment." Put differently, the unauthorized DNS access creates new institutional hostnames, which resolve to infrastructure serving illegal gambling doorway pages. The pages also leverage the established reputation of school and government namespaces to ensure that the malicious URLs show up prominently in search engine results. AI banking credential warning Bank of America is reminding customers not to share banking credentials with AI agents. In an email blast to customers titled "Protecting your finances in the AI World," the financial institution urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, "including an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf." Android tightens contact access Google has announced that an upcoming Android release will no longer be able to directly write to contacts with the WRITE_CONTACTS permission. "Instead, you can use the standard contact intents (ACTION_INSERT, ACTION_EDIT, and ACTION_INSERT_OR_EDIT)," Google said. "Currently, if your app needs to save even one contact, you might be requesting WRITE_CONTACTS. But that permission grants broad access, allowing an app to make widespread changes to contacts across the device in the background, even without user interaction. Most apps don’t need such broad permission." 26,400 live credentials exposed A scan of 7.25 million public repositories on Gitee, China's largest indigenous Git hosting platform, has uncovered 26,400 unique verified-live credentials, including an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform and thousands of live cloud provider access keys, independent security researcher Ben Zimmermann said. Critical Fortinet fixes released Fortinet has released a "coordinated set of security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer" to address critical and high-severity flaws that were flagged using an AI-assisted vulnerability discovery approach. Details of the issues are being kept under wraps until November 10, 2026. With Fortinet devices becoming a favorite target for attackers, it's essential that users move quickly to apply the fixes. Zero-permission token theft Details have emerged about a now-patched flaw in Microsoft Authenticator (CVE-2026-80097 aka AuthMask) that could be exploited by installing and running a malicious application on an affected Android device and convincing the user to complete an authentication flow in the app by claiming to be a trusted app and getting the corresponding tokens. The flaw could be exploited to take over work accounts without requiring additional permissions. "Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to obtain authentication tokens and access resources as the affected user," Microsoft said. According to Enclave, "an unprivileged Android app with zero permissions could impersonate any installed Microsoft first-party app and have the Microsoft Authenticator broker hand it that app's tokens. The setup is a device with Authenticator installed and one work account signed into it." 32 fake AI bots hunt secrets Attackers are disguising themselves as AI agents to steal credentials. Cequence said it has tracked a single actor running AI agent impersonation at scale by posing as about 32 different AI bots, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity, while searching for passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials. "The malicious scanner runs from a major cloud provider and rotates through about 32 AI bot identities, spanning crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Perplexity, and others," Will Glazier said. "It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths. Each address sends a short burst of 50 to 190 requests in about eight seconds and then moves on. The scanner works through targets one at a time, around the clock, and first sends random nonsense paths to find websites that answer every request, a common scanning technique. It hit organizations in financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software, and stayed active from at least late September through late October." China-linked network intrusion The U.S. Embassy in Fiji has revealed that hackers linked to China broke into a regional organization based in Suva between July and August 2026. "Hackers with links to China maintained access to the organization's network over several days," it said. The embassy did not name the threat actor. Nor did it disclose what data the attackers may have accessed. Camera software weaponized Attackers have been breaking into enterprise networks via camera management software, according to new research from security firm Huntress, which observed multiple incidents in September and October 2026 and traced them back to a compromised application. Source code artifacts point to a Korean company selling analog and IP cameras and digital and network video recorders. The activity abuses the legitimate "WpcMon.exe" binary to sideload DLLs that establish outbound connections to a remote server. "This activity demonstrates how attackers can blend malicious code with trusted Windows components to evade detection," Huntress said. 68 GB government data breach In a major operational security blunder, an unknown threat actor stole 68 GB from a Philippine government agency, maintained a detailed log of the transfer, then left that log open on the internet at 13.163.205[.]35:80. "The copy finished in under 24 minutes on September 6, 2026," Hunt.io said. "The transfer log records 27 SQL Server backups whose filenames correspond to the case-management systems of a Philippine overseas-employment and migrant-worker administration. Beside the log sat the operator's toolkit, a rebranded GodPotato build, a PowerShell stager, two payloads and a full Impacket environment." AI model data exfiltration concerns Canadian AI company Cohere has claimed that it caught Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model unsuccessfully attempting to send data to China from its evaluation sandbox as part of a prompt instructing the LLM to detect malicious file download and execution by monitoring for curl processes downloading bash scripts to /tmp followed by bash execution. "Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing," Cohere said. "We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training." Cohere has also released a dataset containing the model trace and corresponding raw token IDs in connection with the behavior. "The exact output is not guaranteed all the time, and many trials may be required to reproduce the behavior," Cohere said, adding "there are similarly unexpected URLs that the model also tends to output, most containing aliyunc." However, the findings have also led to social media chatter that the company is resorting to geopolitical fearmongering and that they are an attempt to clamp down on open-weights models. Post-quantum migration roadmap The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has released guidelines that detail the timelines for transitioning away from quantum-vulnerable algorithms to quantum-resistant standards. "The report describes different use cases and says why one migration might take longer than another," said NIST mathematician Dustin Moody, who heads the PQC standardization project. "We understand there's not one strategy that fits all use cases, and we want to help people handle their migration while staying abreast of what's changing." AI-powered ransomware operation exposed SOCRadar has uncovered the live workspace (i.e., open directory) of a threat actor tied to the n0n ransomware group, which exposed the operation's full workflow as of September 2026. The directory at 185.157.161[.]148 includes an AI coding agent configured with about 150 models to produce hundreds of attack scripts, with more than $7,216 in usage costs. "Entry points included a credential stuffing campaign against 305 FortiGate SSL-VPN devices, exposed AWS keys, weak RDP/WinRM credentials, and compromised hosting management portals," SOCRadar said. At least 23 organizations across 14 countries are said to have been identified in the workspace, including a U.S. sports retailer, a cloud provider, a teachers’ union, a Venezuelan ISP, an Argentine ministry and a pharmaceutical subsidiary. Government AI access restricted The Swedish government has barred employees from accessing browser-based versions of ChatGPT or Claude on their work computers over security concerns relating to the processing of sensitive data. "Officials were concerned that entering sensitive information into these models without an agreement setting out how to protect and secure the data could lead to it being fed into the model and stored for training," Euro News reported. 42 repositories hijacked JFrog and SafeDep have uncovered a campaign in which threat actors hijacked third-party 42 GitHub repositories across 11 owners to deploy payload blobs large enough "to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise." JFrog said, "The repositories contain execution hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, plus 12.9 to 13.7 MB polymorphic wrappers that all decode to the same hidden CI-publisher payload." The activity is assessed to be related to a Miasma-family npm worm propagated under various packages ending with "testmetest." According to SafeDep, the worm "shares code with Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' from June 2026 and adds the token-revocation wiper from Mini Shai-Hulud. The malicious versions steal credentials, spread to other packages and repositories, and install a wiper that deletes the home directory when the victim revokes the stolen GitHub token." Unsuspecting developers who installed the packages had their data stolen and repositories compromised with malicious code to produce further malicious testmetest releases and run shellpanel workflows targeting cPanel systems through CVE-2026-41940, overlapping with a prior campaign detailed by Socket in July 2026. Android banking malware-as-a-service A new Android malware operation called MR ROBOT is targeting customers of Indian banks and transforming banking fraud into a subscription business, with cybercriminals renting customized banking trojans to steal OTPs, card details, UPI PINs and credentials while secretly forwarding calls to bypass security checks. "It is not a single-actor campaign but a rented crimeware platform: a master operator leases access to affiliates, who use a Telegram bot ('APK Shield) and a web control panel (v7.0) to build personalized banking trojans on demand and distribute them through fake Play-Store-style pages and messaging-app lures," CloudSEK said. The kit impersonates around 36 lure apps, including banks, utility providers, and government services. One affiliate is estimated to have intercepted 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices. MDM platforms abused for remote access Threat actors are abusing legitimate mobile device management (MDM) platforms, like Hexnode and Rippling, by using social engineering to enroll devices or install management agents, per Huntress. "Once established, MDM provides a trusted, privileged path for malicious activity, such as deploying rogue RMM tools and maintaining remote access," it said. Critical Gotenberg RCE exploited Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-42589 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical remote code execution flaw in Gotenberg, to deliver a Go-based reverse shell called "cache_base." The flaw was patched in May 2026. According to VulnCheck, the activity originated from a residential Japanese IP address in early October 2026. "The execution flow is straightforward: acquire a lock, collect host information, connect to C2, register the victim, and open a shell," VulnCheck said. Over the past 30 days, the vulnerability has recorded 1,358 exploitation events from 128 unique source IP addresses. Discord discussions go public Discord has announced it will allow search engines to index discussions in Discoverable Servers and make them accessible on the web to users outside the platform without an account or invitation, starting mid-December 2026. "Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you're looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord," it said.
