fj9ffk.text: A flaw in the Linux kernel's TCP code, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, affects Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), and other Linux distributions. The kernel's own CVE team rates it 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. Anthropic said on October 27 that its AI model wrote an exploit that uses the flaw to let a remote attacker with no credentials run commands as root on Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener. As of October 29, Ubuntu and RHEL have not released a fixed kernel. Red Hat, Amazon, Oracle, and SUSE score the flaw between 5.9 and 8.1, lower than the kernel team's 9.8. The flaw is a race condition in the code that sets up new IPv4 TCP connections. It can make the kernel read memory it has already freed, a bug type known as a use-after-free. The kernel fix credits Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge with reporting the bug. Neither the CVE record nor the fix mentions multipath TCP (MPTCP). The link between that feature and this bug comes from Anthropic's post. MPTCP lets one connection use several network paths at once. On Linux, an application must request MPTCP when it opens a socket. Anthropic's post says the flaw "was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches." For distribution users, that fix arrives only in the vendor's kernel package. Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE, and Amazon Linux have shipped fixed packages, at least for some of their kernels, but Ubuntu and RHEL have not. Which Distributions Have a Fix Distribution Vendor rating Status as of October 29 Fixed package or advisory Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, 26.04 LTS and 26.10 Priority High Work in progress None released Ubuntu 16.04, 18.04 and 20.04 Priority High Vulnerable None released RHEL 8, 9 and 10, OpenShift 4 Moderate, 5.9 (CVE page) Important, 8.1 ( advisory file) Fix deferred None released RHEL 7 Not applicable Not affected Not needed Amazon Linux 2023, kernel6.18 package Important, 7.0 Fixed October 24 kernel6.18-6.18.56-125.164.amzn2023 (ALAS2023-2026-3251) Amazon Linux 2023, kernel6.12 package Important, 7.0 Fixed October 29 in Amazon's advisory; Amazon's CVE page still says pending kernel6.12-6.12.113-138.209.amzn2023 (ALAS2023-2026-3335) Amazon Linux 2 Amazon Linux 2023, kernel package Important, 7.0 Pending fix None released Oracle Linux 7, 8, 9 and 10, UEK kernel Important, 8.1 Fixed October 16 ELSA-2026-500397, ELSA-2026-500398, ELSA-2026-500399 Debian trixie (stable) No score listed Fixed October 16 linux 6.12.113-1 (DSA-6568-1) Debian 12 (bookworm) No score listed Fixed October 17 and October 22 linux 6.1.190-1 (DLA-4841-1) linux-6.12 6.12.113-1~deb12u1 (DLA-4850-1) SUSE Linux Micro 6.2, openSUSE Leap 16.0 Important, 8.1 Fixed kernel-default 6.12.0-160000.40.1 or later SLES 15 SP4 to SP6 LTSS, SLES 16.0, SLE Micro 5.3 to 5.5 Important, 8.1 In testing None released SLES 15 SP7 Important, 8.1 Affected, fix in progress None released Ubuntu also lists its cloud, FIPS, and real-time kernels as vulnerable or as work in progress. Red Hat says its fixes are "currently deferred to a future update." Neither Red Hat nor Ubuntu gives a release date. How the Bug Works The race happens during the TCP handshake. When a connection is completed, the kernel hands the IP options stored with the pending request to the new socket without copying them. If that socket is destroyed while another CPU is still using the options to answer a resent connection request, the kernel reads freed memory. IPv6 is not affected by this race because the kernel copies the options for IPv6 connections. The bug was introduced in Linux 4.4. Kernel developers applied a fix on October 5, ten days before the CVE was published. The fix makes the kernel wait until other CPUs finish reading the options before it frees them. Why the Scores Differ The kernel's CVE team added the 9.8 score to the CVE record on October 24, nine days after publishing the CVE. Its score assumes an attacker who sends a TCP connection request carrying IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options, then resends the request to try to win the race. The team rated attack complexity low, saying both sides of the race are "attacker-induced." In that case, the team says, the bug could send nearby kernel memory back to the attacker, corrupt kernel memory, or crash the system. As of October 28, the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) had not added its own score and showed the kernel team's 9.8. Ubuntu's page also shows that score. Red Hat's CVE page rates the flaw Moderate, scoring it 5.9 because the race is hard to win. It says the most likely result is a kernel crash, with memory corruption possible in theory, and that "no confidentiality or integrity impact has been demonstrated." Red Hat's machine-readable advisory file, updated on October 29, lists the impact as Important and scores the flaw 8.1, with high confidentiality and integrity impact. Red Hat's bug tracker changed the issue's severity from medium to high the same day. On that day, the CVE page showed Moderate and 5.9. Oracle and SUSE also score the flaw 8.1, with the same CVSS vector as Red Hat's advisory file. Those scores match the kernel team's on every metric except attack complexity, which the vendors rate high and the kernel team rates low. Amazon scores it 7.0. What Anthropic Says It Built Anthropic described the Linux exploit in an October 27 post about flaws that its AI model, Claude, found and exploited. The Hacker News covered the post on October 28. Claude wrote the exploit after "initial prompting," Anthropic said. The exploit works in two stages. First, the race makes the kernel send extra bytes back to the attacker. Once one of those replies contains a kernel address, the attacker can get around KASLR, the kernel's memory address randomization. Second, the same bug overflows a buffer and overwrites a callback pointer with the address of a payload the attacker had already placed in kernel memory. When the kernel calls that pointer, the payload executes a shell command of the attacker's choice as root. A lost race only fails that one connection attempt and does not crash the system, so an attacker can keep trying, the company said. In its test, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes, and reaching command execution took 5 more minutes. The post does not include the exploit code, the kernel version, or the configuration Anthropic tested. Red Hat says a remote attacker who can reach an exposed TCP service could trigger the race. Anthropic's root exploit, however, targeted servers with a multipath TCP listener. The post does not say whether servers without one can be taken over the same way. As of October 29, none of the vendor advisories, the CVE record, or Anthropic's post reports attacks using the flaw. It does not appear in a copy of CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog that Luxembourg's CIRCL last updated on October 28. What to Do Now Where your distribution has released a fixed kernel, install it. The table above lists the packages and advisories for Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE and Amazon Linux. If you build your own kernel, the fix is in Linux 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. The kernel's CVE team recommends updating to the latest stable kernel. It says the kernel community does not support cherry-picking individual fixes. Ubuntu, RHEL and some Amazon Linux and SUSE releases have no fixed kernel to install yet. Red Hat says no available mitigation meets its standards for being easy to deploy, suitable for most installations and stable. None of the other vendor advisories lists one. The advisories and Anthropic's post do not say whether turning off multipath TCP, or blocking incoming connection requests that carry IP options, would lower the risk.

rkdzos.text: Threat actors are delivering malicious loaders and cryptocurrency miners under the guise of artificial intelligence (AI) desktop applications for Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT as part of a campaign dubbed Yoba. The activity involves creating fake GitHub projects that claim to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus, only to deliver a malware family called YobaLoader. "The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections," Check Point Research said in an analysis. To add to the project's credibility, the attackers set up GitHub.io pages to describe the capabilities of the software. Although the GitHub projects' popularity is not manipulated using techniques like ghost networks, signs point to the use of SEO poisoning tactics to ensure that links to them are surfaced on top of search results on Google. Some of the identified GitHub pages links are below - github[.]com/gpt-5-6/sol-free-desktop gpt-5-6.github[.]io github[.]com/gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io github[.]com/gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io gpt-6-astra[.]github[.]io github[.]com/opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github[.]io opus-5-0[.]github[.]io "Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively," Check Point said. "This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor's true operational time zone." Hosted within these repositories are ZIP archives that, among other files, contain two specific components - Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI Codex or Claude executable winmm.dll, a malicious DLL that's sideloaded by the executable The DLL is a dropper codenamed YobaDropper, which implements checksum value checks by hashing the basename of its host executable and if it matches a hard-coded value "0xE6C2F326." In other words, the check requires it to be launched under "Setup.exe," and fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandboxed environment. Additional anti-analysis techniques and pre-checks include 200,000 iterations of "Sleep(5500)," which amounts to 12.73 days, and skipping machines whose keyboard layout corresponds to that of Russia, Belarus, Tajikistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. Another language ID excluded from the infection process is Tatar. Notably missing from the list is Ukraine, which used to be historically included in such checks. YobaDropper, for its part, triggers a DLL sideloading chain of its own comprising "wmpdmc.exe" and "ampdui.dll," copying the former from its "system32" folder and placing it in a new directory named "WMProcess" created under "ProgramData." The dropper then extracts and decrypts an embedded payload, and drops it into the same folder as "wmpdui.dll." It also establishes persistence by means of a scheduled task that launches the legitimate executable to load the malicious payload. The second DLL is YobaLoader. It implements the same anti-sandbox technique as YobaDropper, requiring the malware to be run only by "wmpdmc.exe" by checking the hash against a hard-coded value ("0x552751E3"). The loader is responsible for three main tasks - Downloads an image from a Telegram channel ("t[.]me/yoba_fanclub"). Uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words and an integer value in the range 0–999 using a domain generation algorithm (DGA). The end result is domain in the format "adjective-noun-verb-digit.dedyn[.]io." Queries Google's DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain a Base64-encoded command from a DNS TXT record by passing the constructed domain as input. Decrypts the response to obtain the link to fetch the next-stage payload ("files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat"). "By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity," Check Point said. The downloaded payload is then injected into "svchost.exe," resulting in the execution of an XMRig cryptocurrency miner. Evidence indicates that the first GitHub repository was created around July 2026, although the malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August. What's more, early versions of YobaLoader have been found to only exclude Russia from infection, while also incorporating extensive anti-debugging and anti-VM checks, which have since been removed in newer versions. "The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance," Check Point said. "By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious."

b2sg4z.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 29, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cybersecurity Google on Wednesday took the wraps off Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities. "It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching," Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president of Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, said. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index benchmark, Carbon leads with a score of 59, surpassing Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (58), OpenAI GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55). One of the core focus areas is cybersecurity, where the latest iteration reportedly delivers significant performance improvements across the board, including vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also twice as likely to generate secure code versus Argon. Google also emphasized that Carbon attempts to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks by seeking human input in the face of ambiguity rather than "guessing or forcing a path forward," as well as resisting every evaluated attack attempt at indirect prompt injection. The debut of Gemini 4 Carbon comes less than a week after the tech giant unveiled Gemini 4 Argon. The release plan is similar to that of its predecessor, with the rollout currently limited to a subset of cyber defenders before expanding access to other trusted partners as part of its Fairwind Program. Google also said it's actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing. The development comes as OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, which it described as a fast, efficient model that "excels at communication and computer-based tasks." "GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra," OpenAI said. "GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user's task." Earlier this week, rival Anthropic also disclosed that an unreleased, internal research model uncovered critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used software. This included a one-click remote code execution in Google Chrome, a one-click exploit chain in Apple Safari that could be used to access a user's browsing history, cookies, and other sensitive data, an Android lock screen bypass, and a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw in the Windows HTTP.sys driver (CVE-2026-33096, CVSS score: 7.5). All the identified issues have been fixed by Google, Apple, and Microsoft. "These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic said. "These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

1kwmvaz.text: The Hacker NewsOct 29, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Webinar Security teams have spent years trying to detect threats faster. AI is changing the harder part: how much time defenders have left to act. Advanced AI models can now help attackers discover vulnerabilities, generate exploit code, and move through weaknesses faster than traditional security processes were built to handle. The challenge is no longer just finding another vulnerability or generating another alert. It is knowing which exposures matter, what an attacker can reach, and which issues need to be fixed first. That is the focus of next week's webinar, How to Build AI Threat Readiness Across Your Security Operations, featuring an expert from Wiz. The session will show how security teams can improve visibility, prioritize real risk, and shorten the path from detection to remediation. Most security teams already have plenty of data. They have vulnerability findings, cloud alerts, identity signals, application telemetry, and threat detections. The harder problem is connecting those signals quickly enough to answer the questions that drive action. Is this vulnerability reachable? Does the exposed asset contain sensitive data? Can an attacker move from it to something more important? Who owns the affected system? What should be fixed first? When those answers live across different tools and teams, investigations slow down. That delay matters more when attackers can automate parts of the discovery and exploitation process. The webinar focuses on two practical needs: broad visibility and faster action. Security teams need enough context to understand risk across cloud infrastructure, code, identities, SaaS, AI services, and the software supply chain. They also need a way to identify exploitable paths, investigate suspicious activity, and deliver remediation to the right owner without having to rebuild the same context every time. A Wiz expert will explain how organizations can use unified security context to separate urgent exposure from background noise, understand attack paths, and bring security agents into investigation and remediation workflows. For SOC teams, that can mean less time spent manually assembling context. For vulnerability management, it means knowing which findings deserve immediate attention. For cloud and security engineering teams, it means connecting risk to the people and systems that can actually fix it. The goal is not to automate every security decision. It is to remove delays caused by fragmented tools, repetitive investigation, and unclear ownership. Attendees will leave with a framework for assessing whether their current security operations are ready for faster, AI-assisted attacks. The key questions are practical: Can you see enough of the environment to understand an attack path? Can you quickly determine whether a new issue affects something attackers can reach? Can you move a validated risk from detection to remediation fast enough? AI is increasing the speed at which weaknesses can be found and used. Security teams need to respond with better context and less delay.

14ic6cu.text: A flaw in Telegram for Android allowed an attacker to run code on a victim's phone via a voice call once the victim answered, according to security startup NebuSec. The attacker needed only an ordinary Telegram account. Telegram fixed the flaw in version 12.10.4 of the app, released in late September, and NebuSec disclosed it on October 29. The flaw can be triggered in every version from 8.6.2 through 12.10.3, NebuSec's co-founder and chief executive said in an email to The Hacker News. Those versions came out between March 2022 and September 2026. The company confirmed it in private phone calls on ARM64-based phones and has no evidence so far that it directly affects Telegram's iOS and desktop apps or group calls. Anyone using Telegram for Android should make sure the app is on version 12.10.4 or later. The version number appears at the bottom of the app's Settings page. The flaw had no CVE identifier as of October 29. The Hacker News has asked NebuSec and Telegram whether the flaw was used in real attacks, and asked NebuSec what an attacker's code could reach on a phone. During a Telegram call, the two apps send each other short messages to set up the call and report its state. One type, called MediaState, reports whether the microphone is muted, whether the camera is on, and how the video is rotated. The flaw was in the code that reads MediaState messages. That code did not handle missing fields correctly and accessed memory it should not, according to NebuSec. Telegram's published source code for version 12.10.3 contains a flaw that matches that description, a review by The Hacker News found. When a MediaState message included a rotation value, the code checked that value. It then read a different field, the video state, even if the message had no such field. Version 12.10.4 reads the rotation value from the right field. The calling code that uses this message was switched on in version 8.6.2, the first version NebuSec names. Telegram's Android, iOS, and desktop apps use one shared library, called tgcalls, for calls. A change labeled "Fix camera rotation" made the same correction in tgcalls on April 21, 2026. Telegram's iOS source code included that change from version 12.7, released in May, and the desktop app's code from version 7.0.1, released in July. Telegram for Android received it in version 12.10.4 in September. Whether the earlier code could be exploited in those apps has not been shown. NebuSec's video shows two phones, one marked as the attacker and one as the victim. The victim accepts a Telegram call. About half a minute into the call, the victim's phone switches to its home screen, the app icons fall down the screen, and a "HACKED BY NEBUSEC" logo appears. The video does not show which Telegram or Android version the victim's phone was running. No technical write-up of the flaw was on NebuSec's website as of October 29, so the step from the flaw to running code depends on the video and on what the company says. NebuSec, a startup backed by Y Combinator, says its Code Security product, which runs on OpenAI's GPT-5.4 model, found the flaw. In July, the company described an Android exploit chain that started with a Firefox flaw and reached the kernel of an ARM64 device running Android 17. Separately, the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) published an advisory on October 15 about an unpatched flaw in rlottie, the library Telegram apps have used to draw animated stickers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111105 (CVSS score: 7.0), can let an attacker run code if a user opens a malicious file or page, ZDI said. Telegram had told ZDI in March that checks on its servers mitigated the flaw, and in April asked ZDI for a full remote code execution chain. Those checks could be bypassed, researcher Saifeldeen Aziz says in the abstract for his OffensiveCon talk in Tokyo. The research used AI-guided fuzzing, which feeds code with large amounts of broken or unexpected input, to find memory-corruption bugs in rlottie across Telegram's iOS, Android, and desktop apps. It then chained those bugs, which stem from flaws in how stickers are delivered and checked, to run code on Telegram for iOS. The Android app replaced rlottie with tlottie, a library written in Rust, between versions 12.8.1 in June and 12.10.0 in August, according to Telegram's published source code. The desktop app's code made the same switch in September, and the iOS code added tlottie in version 13.0 in October while still including rlottie.

1oodlak.text: AI is beginning to take over much of the work that has traditionally defined the security analyst's job. Investigating alerts, collecting evidence, correlating activity across tools, and executing response actions are becoming tasks that AI systems can perform on their own. As these capabilities mature, security operations centers (SOCs) will see major changes in how work is organized, how decisions are made, and what is expected of the people responsible for defending organizations. For security professionals, this is a chance to take on a much broader role. As AI assumes more of the operational workload, analysts can move beyond individual alerts and investigations to direct the defense across the entire security lifecycle. We call this emerging role the Threat Operator: an AI-native security professional who translates business risk into defensive priorities, directs AI-driven operations, and exercises judgment over the decisions and actions taken by those systems. The impact reaches beyond day-to-day SOC work. It will change the skills organizations need, how security professionals develop expertise, and the career paths open to people entering the field. From Individual Tasks to Overall Defense The traditional SOC developed around specialized functions, each supported by its own tools and workflows. Threat intelligence teams study adversaries, detection engineers create rules, threat hunters search for activity that existing controls may have missed, analysts investigate alerts, and incident responders contain confirmed threats. These functions are closely related, yet the work often moves between teams through separate systems, tickets, and manual handoffs. AI is starting to tie these activities together. For example, intelligence about a new threat can lead to a hunting hypothesis, which can reveal a detection gap and produce a new detection. That detection may identify suspicious activity requiring investigation, followed by containment and further improvements to the organization's defenses. AI agents can coordinate and execute these workflows, carrying context and findings from one stage to the next. That changes where security professionals add the most value. A Threat Operator works across the defensive lifecycle, setting priorities based on the organization's exposure, business operations, and threat landscape. They determine which risks deserve attention, what the defense should accomplish, how much autonomy AI should have, and when a decision requires human intervention. They are also responsible for judging whether the operation is actually improving security. Consider a financial institution facing a newly identified threat targeting identity infrastructure. AI agents could assess the institution's exposure, hunt for relevant activity, identify gaps in existing detections, and recommend defensive actions. The Threat Operator would provide the institutional context needed to guide that work, including which systems support critical business processes, what constitutes unacceptable risk, and which actions require authorization. The result is a gradual shift from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop, with security professionals supervising and governing AI-driven operations. The level of autonomy will depend on the maturity of the technology, the consequences of particular actions, and the organization's tolerance for risk, but a human remains accountable throughout. Rethinking How Security Professionals Gain Experience Junior security analysts will feel some of the biggest effects. For decades, the SOC has provided an entry point into cybersecurity, with analysts developing their skills through alert triage, evidence collection, investigations, documentation, and escalation. Although much of this work is repetitive, it has also served as an apprenticeship. Over time, analysts learn how systems behave, how attackers operate, and how experienced practitioners distinguish genuine threats from benign activity. As AI absorbs more of these responsibilities, organizations will need to rethink how that experience is acquired. The traditional progression from handling simple alerts to managing complex investigations may become less relevant as AI takes on more sophisticated work. Without a deliberate approach to training, security teams may struggle to develop the experienced professionals they will need in the future. AI can also open up a different path for professional development. Junior Threat Operators can gain supervised exposure to a much wider range of security activities, examining how intelligence informs hunting, how detections are developed, how investigations reach conclusions, and how response decisions affect the business. They can review the evidence behind AI-generated findings, challenge assumptions, identify missing context, and learn from the decisions made by more experienced colleagues. This only works if organizations invest in technical fundamentals and structured mentorship. Analysts still need to understand networks, operating systems, attacker techniques, and the security technologies underlying AI-driven workflows. Experienced practitioners will need to teach younger colleagues how to evaluate conclusions, recognize uncertainty, and exercise judgment when the available evidence is incomplete. The Skills Needed For the current generation of security analysts, technical proficiency has often been measured through familiarity with security tools and the ability to extract useful information from them. Query languages, detection logic, endpoint telemetry, and investigation techniques have been central to the profession. Those skills still matter. AI adds new demands on top of them: orchestration, governance, and interpreting automated decisions. Threat Operators will need to translate business security risks into clear defensive objectives that AI systems can execute. They must understand the organization's architecture, critical assets, operational dependencies, and relevant adversaries, and know how to communicate that context to AI agents. Their work will involve evaluating hypotheses, validating evidence, setting escalation criteria, and determining whether an automated action has achieved its intended outcome. For example, an AI system investigating a compromised server may recommend immediate isolation. That call could be technically sound. But the server may support a critical business process where disruption carries significant consequences. A Threat Operator must understand those dependencies and determine how the response should proceed, balancing containment requirements with operational risk. This need for defined oversight and accountability is also reflected in the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The role will combine four areas of expertise: Business security risk: Understanding organizational priorities, critical assets, and the consequences of security decisions. Threat and adversary understanding: Interpreting intelligence and anticipating how attackers may target the environment. wmb22b.text: 26,400 credentials that developers left in public code on Gitee, a Chinese code-hosting service, still worked when a researcher tested them. Anyone who copied one from that code could have used it. Independent researcher Ben Zimmermann found them by scanning 7.25 million public Gitee repositories and reported the results on October 28. Most were keys for cloud and AI services, led by 9,473 Alibaba Cloud AccessKey pairs. Zimmermann sent the vendors with the most exposed keys a list of their credentials, but he did not contact the developers who leaked them. When he published, he had not confirmed that any of the reported credentials had been revoked. So anyone who has pushed a key to a public Gitee repository cannot assume it has been revoked. The scan ran for about a month, but Zimmermann did not provide the dates, so it is unclear how long ago the credentials were tested. He also did not say whether anyone else had used them. He ran two secret scanners, TruffleHog and Kingfisher, over every repository. Both tried each credential against the service that issued it and kept only those that worked, he wrote. The scanners read each repository's full commit history. A key that a developer later removed from the code could still be found and counted there. The 26,400 figure counts each credential once, regardless of how many repositories it appeared in. By commit date, 12,242 of the credentials came from 2025, nearly half the total. Some dated to the late 2000s. What Was Exposed After the Alibaba Cloud keys, the largest groups were 3,805 YouTube API keys, 3,170 DeepSeek keys, 1,489 keys for Zhipu's BigModel AI platform, and 1,348 OpenAI keys. Smaller numbers were found for GitHub, AWS, Google Cloud and Google's Gemini. One of the credentials was "an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform," Zimmermann wrote. He did not name the platform or say what the credential could reach. What a working key lets someone do depends on the service. OpenAI says that a compromised key allows another person to use the account's quota without the owner's consent. That can cause "data loss, unexpected charges," a used-up monthly quota, and interrupted API access. A YouTube API key is a Google Cloud API key that identifies a project, Google says. Without API restrictions, such a key can be used with every API that accepts Google Cloud keys. What to Do If You Committed Keys Treat any key that has ever been in a public Gitee repository as exposed, and revoke it at the provider. Deleting a key from the code or rewriting the repository's history does not revoke it, as noted by TruffleHog's maker, Truffle Security. Alibaba Cloud: create a new AccessKey pair, switch your apps to it, then disable and delete the old pair. Check for unexpected charges and for resources created or deleted that you did not need, Alibaba Cloud's leak response plan says. ActionTrail shows the key's API calls for the last 90 days, but data operations in services such as OSS and SLS have to be checked in each service's own logs. Google and YouTube API keys: rotate the key, which creates a new key with the same restrictions, update your apps to use it, then delete the old key. Add API restrictions so the key works only with the APIs you need. OpenAI: rotate the key immediately from the API Keys page, as OpenAI advises, and set spend limits to help limit charges from a leaked key. Two Scanners, Different Results MongoDB makes Kingfisher, and Zimmermann's post was developed with its Kingfisher team. In this scan, TruffleHog found 12,737 credentials that worked, and Kingfisher found 14,664, but only 1,001 were found by both. Each tool alone found about half of the total. TruffleHog found almost all of the Alibaba Cloud keys. Kingfisher found all 1,489 BigModel keys, because TruffleHog has no detector for Zhipu's keys, Zimmermann wrote. Teams that rely on a single scanner should verify its detectors against the services they use. Gitee and Other Code Hosts China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology chose Gitee in 2020 as the base for a national open-source code-hosting platform. Gitee's public API is limited, and a 2021 attempt to study leaked credentials on the site gave up because of it. Gitee's rate, 3.64 working credentials per 1,000 repositories scanned, is higher than the rates from earlier scans of GitLab (3.11) and Bitbucket (2.39). Those scans used only TruffleHog, Zimmermann wrote. Based on TruffleHog's results alone, Gitee's rate is 1.76, but that count excludes services TruffleHog does not cover, such as Zhipu. So neither figure shows which platform leaks more.

18rwc5.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 29, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Cisco has released patches to address a high-severity security flaw in Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software that it said has been exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-76418, is rated 8.6 on the CVSS scoring system. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition. According to Cisco, the issue is rooted in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of ASA and FTD software. "This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group," it said in a Wednesday advisory. "An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the affected device to reload, resulting in a DoS condition." The network equipment major said it became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability in October 2026, but did not share any specifics as to when the attacks began, who is behind them, and the scale of the efforts. Fixes for the flaw are available in the following versions - Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software Release 9.16 and earlier - Fixed in 9.16.4.104 9.18 - Fixed in 9.18.4.96 9.20 - Fixed in 9.20.4.50 9.22 - Fixed in 9.22.3.200 9.23 - Fixed in 9.23.1.48 9.24 - Fixed in 9.24.1.27 and 9.24.10.1 Cisco Secure FTD Software Release 7.0 and earlier - Fixed in 7.0.11 7.2 - Fixed in 7.2.13 7.4 - Fixed in 7.4.9 7.6 - Fixed in 7.6.7 7.7 - Fixed in 7.7.14 10.0 - Fixed in 10.0.3 10.1 - Fixed in 10.1.1 Cisco also noted that the vulnerability affects Cisco devices if the following conditions are met - They are running a vulnerable release of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software or Cisco Secure FTD Software. The SSL remote access VPN login service is reachable. Secondary authentication is configured in the tunnel group scope. "If tunnel-group-list enable is configured, check all tunnel groups, including the default tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup, for secondary-authentication-server-group," Cisco said. "If tunnel-group-list enable is absent or has been removed using the no tunnel-group-list enable command, check the default tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup, for secondary-authentication-server-group because disabling the group list does not remove exposure when that default group uses secondary authentication." As a temporary mitigation, the company is recommending that customers turn off the tunnel group list if DefaultWEBVPNGroup does not use secondary authentication, or disable secondary authentication on any user-configured tunnel group list or on the default tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup. "On Cisco Secure FTD Software, review the deployed remote access VPN policy and the resulting device running configuration in Cisco Secure FMC Software or Cisco Secure FDM," Cisco said. "A successful VPN login is not required to reach the affected processing path." The disclosure comes as Cisco revealed that a sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor tracked as UAT-11473 weaponized CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controller instances, to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to affected systems. The activity, which has targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research sectors, is assessed to share infrastructure overlaps with Volt Typhoon's Silent Train covert network. "UAT-11473 then installed a custom malware framework we track as 'KeyDrift' consisting of multiple components [like PolyFlame and LittleFilch] geared towards collecting sensitive keying information, acting as backdoors and intermediate command-and-control (C2) hosts," Cisco Talos said. "The framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material. KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records."

1mol1hm.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 29, 2026DevSecOps / Vulnerability GitHub has announced that it's introducing a new package firewall as a preview to block installation of suspicious npm packages during installation time. "The firewall inspects both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity, acting as an install-time policy gate," GitHub said. The feature, which currently supports only npm packages, is available in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud. According to the Microsoft subsidiary, the firewall is placed between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories so as to deter malware attacks that compromise systems when packages are installed. This behavior can expose users to severe security risks, especially when artificial intelligence (AI) agents and CI runners automatically install dependencies to complete a task or build without their explicit permission. The idea is that endpoints like coding agents and CI/CD hosts use the firewall for their requests instead of directly pointing to the public package registries. The firewall then checks package downloads against policy controls such as minimum package age and malware advisories, and blocks downloads that do not meet those policies. To use the firewall, administrators are required to configure policy controls, such as the ones listed below - Block known malware by checking against the GitHub Advisory Database for active malware advisories Block packages based on the severity of vulnerabilities by checking the GitHub Advisory Database for flaws that affect the requested package version. The control defaults to "Critical only" as the severity level that blocks an installation, although users can choose "High or higher," "Medium or higher," or "Any severity." Block attestation downgrades by comparing attestations for the requested package version with those of earlier versions and stop the download if the requested version does not have an SLSA attestation. Block newly-introduced install scripts by checking whether the package recently added scripts that run using preinstall or postinstall hooks, which can be abused to steal sensitive data. Block packages based on a cooldown period that prevents versions that are newer than the configured minimum age from being installed. The value can range from 1 to 365 days. The default value is 1 day. Users can disable it by setting it to 0. Users who need access to a package that gets blocked erroneously by the firewall can submit an exception request, which can then be approved by enterprise administrators and security managers. The development comes as Rust 1.100, which is scheduled for release on November 12, 2026, readies to add support for a configurable minimum publish age, allowing security scanners and maintainers time to flag and block malicious crate releases before they can be installed or used by users. The value, defined via the "global-min-publish-age" option in "cargo/config.toml," allows users to specify a minimum publication age in days or weeks. If left unspecified, a seven-day waiting period is applied by default to skip releases published within that window. Over the past year, similar waiting periods have been implemented across open-source ecosystems, including npm, Python, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, Ruby, Bun, pnpm, and Yarn, as a way to bolster software supply chain security by reducing the chance that a newly published, unreviewed version is immediately pulled into a build. Cooldown periods help add friction and slow down attacks in which a bad actor publishes a poisoned version of a popular package after seizing control of a maintainer account, thereby preventing rapid spread through manual or automated installations. "The tradeoff is that legitimate fixes have to wait, too, unless developers make an exception," Socket said. "Malicious code also doesn't magically become harmless with age. A release that escapes detection can simply outlast the cooldown. The value is in buying researchers, maintainers, and registries time to act before the next dependency update carries an attack further."

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. oapp2e.text: Anthropic has introduced OSS Scanner, a free service that checks critical open-source repositories for security vulnerabilities and sends findings directly to project maintainers. The opt-in program uses the company’s strongest AI models to run repeated scans, giving developers a faster route to potential flaws without waiting for human review. According to Anthropic’s service overview, OSS Scanner builds on its work with Project Glasswing. The company says it had reviewed more than 6,000 vulnerability reports by October 2026 through its existing disclosure process. The new service offers a separate path for projects willing to assess AI-generated reports. Anthropic OSS Scanner According to the GitHub repository, the scanner first builds an enrolled project inside an isolated virtual machine with network access enabled. This stage installs dependencies and prepares the software for testing. Anthropic then removes Internet access before the security audit begins, allowing scanning agents to examine the project within a restricted environment. Reports arrive by email with steps to reproduce the suspected issue and a proposed patch where available. Anthropic says its pipeline includes agents that double-check bugs and examine their root causes. However, these checks are automated. A human does not review the findings before maintainers receive them. After the first scan, the service checks projects again for newly introduced vulnerabilities and issues missed earlier. Scan frequency depends on factors such as demand and project usage. This extends Anthropic’s wider push into security research, including earlier work in which Claude uncovered 22 Firefox vulnerabilities. Core maintainers apply through the official GitHub repository by opening a pull request that adds a directory under projects/<name>. Each submission needs a project.yaml configuration containing the repository address and a primary contact email. Anthropic manually checks that applicants are core maintainers before accepting a project. Eligibility focuses on established projects with broad use, exposure to remote attacks, and significant infrastructure security impact. A Dockerfile must explain how to install dependencies and build the software. Developers can keep it in their own repository or beside project.yaml in the enrollment repository. Everything needed for building and testing must be downloaded during setup because the later audit cannot access the Internet. An optional threat_model.md file helps guide the scan. Maintainers can describe where untrusted input enters, which components are outside scope, and how they rate severity. They can also explain preferred report formats and patch requirements, reducing the need for the scanner to guess project-specific security expectations. Before applying, developers can use tools/validate.py to check their configuration and tools/check <name> to test the build. The checking tool runs with network access, so Anthropic warns users to test only trusted projects or use a separate machine. Configuration email addresses are public, making a dedicated security alias useful. Maintainers can add an OpenPGP public key for encrypted reports, but encrypted messages go only to the primary contact and cannot include additional recipients. Anthropic does not impose a 90-day disclosure deadline on unvalidated findings. However, a report later confirmed through its human-reviewed program may enter that disclosure process. This safeguard matters amid concerns about AI-generated vulnerability reports wasting maintainers’ time. Project owners still need to reproduce suspected flaws and test suggested fixes before treating them as confirmed vulnerabilities. Reports can be paused with disabled: true, while deleting the enrollment directory withdraws the project entirely Cut every SOC alert investigation by 21 min. 1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink. j5jng0.text: Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, warning that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. Its October 8 guidance says the shift will affect applications, devices, certificate chains, and the processes that keep digital trust working. The message goes beyond protecting encrypted traffic. While many quantum security plans focus on attackers collecting data now to decrypt later, authentication depends on certificates and private keys being issued, stored, checked, renewed, and managed across different vendors. Changing the underlying algorithms can expose gaps across that entire chain. Microsoft Security Researchs noted that organizations often know where TLS protects communications but lack a complete view of certificate dependencies. Their report concerns infrastructure readiness, not a newly discovered malware campaign. Post-Quantum Authentication The main challenge is not simply finding a quantum-resistant algorithm. Businesses must establish whether their existing systems can use new certificates reliably. Older PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, custom applications, and third-party services may contain fixed assumptions that only become visible during testing. Larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains can affect connection setup, storage, transmission, and network inspection limits. Related work on Cloudflare’s post-quantum certificate authority shows why certificate size and connection speed matter as providers explore different designs for quantum-safe authentication. Those efforts do not remove the need to test enterprise systems individually. HSM providers and security appliance vendors therefore belong in the migration discussion from the start. Teams need to check whether hardware-backed systems support future certificate requirements and whether monitoring, inspection, and certificate-management tools can process the resulting traffic. Support in one application does not establish readiness across the full environment. Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Microsoft launched its Post-Quantum Cryptography TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026. It allows approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to test certificate roots and issuance using ML-DSA-87, a quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm. The focus is compatibility, performance, and day-to-day operations. The August release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com. Admissions continue through the end of 2026. Microsoft’s published authentication readiness guidance directs eligible providers to the Trusted Root Program portal for requirements and applications. These certificates are not publicly trusted. Microsoft limits their use to closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds, explicitly excluding production trust and public-facing websites. Elsewhere, Let’s Encrypt’s certificate roadmap explores Merkle Tree Certificates for public-web authentication, highlighting that separate efforts are addressing different parts of the transition. On supported, correctly configured Windows 11 systems, pilot testing begins with the July 28, 2026 updates. Microsoft names KB5101681, OS Build 28000.2608, for 26H1, and KB5101684, OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973, for 25H2. ML-DSA certificates can also work with Secure Channel, or Schannel, in supported scenarios. Administrators must confirm platform requirements before testing. Software and hardware readiness should be checked separately. Earlier coverage of Google’s quantum-safe digital signatures described software-based Cloud KMS support with hardware-backed support planned separately. Microsoft similarly urges organizations to ask certificate providers, HSM vendors, software suppliers, and platform vendors about their roadmaps and testing capabilities rather than assume universal support. Security teams should inventory certificate-dependent systems, map public and private trust relationships, and identify equipment with long upgrade cycles. Non-production tests should cover compatibility, performance, and operational workflows. Developments such as OpenSSL’s post-quantum performance improvements offer useful testing context, but preview software and Microsoft’s pilot certificates should not be treated as production-ready replacements. That work should include the full certificate lifecycle, not just a successful connection. Issuance, distribution, validation, renewal, and management all depend on linked systems. Testing those steps together helps teams find process gaps that a standalone algorithm test could miss before they reach live business services. Microsoft recommends a multi-year program with named owners, clear dependencies, and modernization priorities based on test results. Organizations can ask their certificate provider whether it participates in the pilot and offers suitable testing. The practical goal is to uncover failures before quantum-resistant authentication becomes a large-scale deployment requirement. 6tjopr.text: VirusTotal has added daily scanning of the public IPv4 space, giving security teams a new way to find command-and-control (C2) servers and track malware infrastructure. Announced on October 8, 2026, the update records exposed services, port activity, banners, and server fingerprints alongside existing threat intelligence. The change helps researchers look beyond an IP address’s detection score. Earlier reports showed hosting details, passive DNS records, and files that contacted an address. The new data shows what a server exposes now, helping analysts find related hosts that have no malware detections. A new Ports tab lists open, closed, and recently closed ports, together with service names, software versions, and timestamps. Records also include SSH host keys, RDP fingerprints, HTTP headers, and operating system details inferred from service responses. VirusTotal keeps records when ports stop responding. Researchers can therefore check when a suspected C2 service was last seen online and compare that date with changes elsewhere in a campaign. This history adds context that a current detection score cannot provide. VirusTotal Adds Daily Internet Scanning The official announcement describes searches through the web interface and API. Queries such as entity:ip open_port:22 find exposed SSH services. Bracket syntax ties conditions to specific ports, preventing a product on one port from being incorrectly matched with a version on another. These searches build on the methods covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal threat research guide. One investigation started with 91.219.237[.]110, an address listed in APT28 and Havoc collections. Its SSH fingerprint led researchers to 185.146.232[.]3, which had no detections, collections, or communicating files. Both hosts shared an OpenSSH build, nginx configuration, and an unusual certificate name, b4ck.my. Searching that certificate name uncovered a third address, 96.9.125[.]59. Port timestamps suggested one server was being retired around the time another appeared. However, VirusTotal warned that older malware links do not establish current ownership or APT28 attribution because IP addresses can change hands. Fingerprint matches also need careful checks. Some SSH keys appeared across more than 1,400 cloud addresses because server templates reused them. An open port alone is similarly weak evidence. Searching Cobalt Strike’s default team server port returned over 1.5 million addresses, including hosts answering on many ports. Another example exposed a NOX Stealer login panel at 5.175.221[.]206 on port 8443. The host also exposed SMB and RDP, with scan data identifying Windows Server 2022, nginx 1.24.0, and PHP 8.3.33. Combining those traits reduced a search from 4.5 million hosts to ten candidates, not ten confirmed malicious servers. When the panel changed its name to BOMBAY Stealer, browser analysis captured the new title while the exposed services stayed unchanged. Researchers also searched FTP banners containing “conhost,” finding five addresses tied to command-delivery patterns discussed in E4del and PINHOLE research. Port data is available through API records and history endpoints, but not yet through IP Livehunt rules. Saved searches run on a schedule offer a workaround. fow618.text: Alleged internal chats from Silent Ransom Group suggest the criminals collected $206.95 million from 27 firms in roughly six months without encrypting victims’ files. The reported earnings point to the power of data extortion, where attackers steal sensitive records and demand payment to keep them private. However, the payment figures remain unverified, and the group denies breaching its systems or leaking its chats. DataBreaches reported the alleged leak on October 7. The material contains 5,692 messages covering August 27, 2025, through September 29, 2026. Discussions reportedly include victim negotiations, payments, access methods, and members’ spending. An October 8 update said Silent Ransom Group had agreed to an interview but disputed the leak’s origin. Silent Ransomware Extorted Over $200,000,000 The chats mark completed deals as “GOLD.” Adding those entries produces the $206.95 million total. Crystal Intelligence dates the 27 claimed payments between April 3 and September 24, 2026, placing the reported earnings within a period of less than six months. These entries reflect the criminals’ own records, not audited financial results. According to DataBreaches, the median alleged payment was $6 million, while individual amounts ranged from $100,000 to $30 million. White & Case was listed against the largest amount. Nine named firms disclosed breaches relevant to the period. However, those disclosures do not confirm who attacked them or whether they paid the sums shown. Crystal Intelligence’s blockchain analysis found transactions matching the timing of several chat entries. One upstream collection wallet received about 344 bitcoin, valued at roughly $27 million, over six weeks. Researchers could not connect individual victim payments to that wallet. Hence, the evidence supports substantial money movement rather than proving the headline total. Operators trick employees into granting access, steal documents, and threaten to publish them. Law firms have been a major focus because they hold private client information. CybersecurityNews previously covered the group’s IT support impersonation attacks against law firms. Attackers call employees, pose as internal support staff, and persuade them to grant remote access. Legitimate software helps the activity blend into routine work, reducing reliance on malware that security tools might otherwise detect. Related reporting on Luna Moth’s fake helpdesk domains describes websites designed to resemble company support services. Once they gain access, tools such as WinSCP and Rclone can transfer stolen files. The pressure comes from the possible disclosure of confidential records, not a sudden loss of access to business systems. Crystal found instructions to use fresh wallets, keep victim funds separate, and avoid combining payouts. Operators sometimes broke those rules, linking transactions investigators could trace. Smaller payments also reached regulated exchanges, creating potential leads through customer identity records. The analysis describes cash conversion through instant exchangers, couriers, and a Bitcoin-to-Zelle service. For defenders, the attack chain makes identity checks essential. Employees should verify support requests through known internal channels before granting access. Organizations should restrict remote access, deploy phishing-resistant authentication, and train staff to recognize phone-based deception. Working systems don’t prove sensitive files stay safe. 1w6ljoy.text: A malicious Android PDF reader distributed through Google Play has recorded more than 10,000 installs while serving as an installer for the Anatsa banking trojan. The finding shows how a routine document tool can become a route for malware that puts banking passwords and financial accounts at risk. The installation figure describes the reach of the reader app, not a confirmed count of successful banking infections or stolen accounts. The available alert also does not identify affected banks, victim countries, financial losses, or whether Google has since removed this particular listing, wile those details remain unconfirmed. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the malicious installer and shared its indicators in an October 8 alert on X. They described the application as an Android PDF reader with over 10,000 installs and published separate file hashes for the installer and the Anatsa payload, alongside their command-and-control addresses. The discovery follows earlier cases involving similar disguises. In April, a fake document reader campaign used a different package to distribute Anatsa before Google removed that app. That earlier removal should not be confused with the status of the newly reported reader, which the current alert does not establish. Malicious PDF Reader With 10,000+ Installs Anatsa, also known as TeaBot, uses a dropper model: the app installed first acts as a delivery tool for a separate malicious component. This separation helps explain why a download that appears useful can later expose a phone to banking malware. The latest alert identifies both stages but does not provide a full execution trace. In its technical analysis of Anatsa, ThreatLabz documented earlier campaigns that downloaded additional code and presented the final payload as an app update. Some samples checked the device environment before proceeding, helping the malware avoid test systems used by researchers. These are documented family techniques, not confirmed findings for every new sample. ThreatLabz also documented malformed APK archive headers that made older payloads harder to inspect, along with encrypted code loaded at runtime. APK files are Android installation packages; hiding their contents can disrupt tools that inspect files without running them. The new alert does not confirm whether these samples use those methods. The broader use of Google Play stealth loaders shows why unexpected update requests deserve attention even when the original app came from an official store. A request to install an extra component outside the normal update process can move the user from a harmless-looking utility to the banking payload. ThreatLabz has uncovered another new Anatsa installer that is distributed via the Google Play Store. The application is disguised as an Android PDF reader that currently has over 10,000 installs. The IOCs for this campaign are listed below: Google Play Store URL… pic.twitter.com/duQA0myTAi — Zscaler ThreatLabz (@Threatlabz) October 8, 2026 For this campaign, ThreatLabz listed one installer-related command-and-control URL and two payload command-and-control endpoints. Keeping those roles separate matters during an investigation: the installer and the banking trojan are different files, and each has its own published MD5 hash. The alert does not explain the exact contents returned by the installer URL. Why Banking Accounts Are at Risk Earlier ThreatLabz research found that Anatsa requested SMS and accessibility permissions, contacted its control server, and checked for targeted financial apps. The server then supplied fake login pages matching apps on the phone. Credentials entered into those pages were sent to the attackers rather than the bank. A previous Anatsa document reader outbreak reached more than 100,000 downloads and used fake banking screens to capture account details. That history explains the concern around this new reader, but its target list and permission behavior still require sample-specific verification rather than assumptions based on older campaigns. What Android Users Should Do Users who installed the identified reader should remove it, review granted permissions, and scan their phones with a trusted security tool. Keep Google Play Protect enabled and question unexpected requests for SMS or accessibility access. If banking activity looks suspicious, contact the bank promptly and change account passwords from a trusted device. For security teams, the package name can support app inventory checks, while file hashes help match samples against the reported installer and payload. Network logs can be searched for the listed domain and IP endpoints. Matches should be reviewed in context to establish which device communicated, when contact occurred, and whether malware executed. 1gei1bk.text: Google along with several cybersecurity companies and Japanese law enforcement dismantled a global botnet called X.CPE that was hidden in more than 1.3 million set-top boxes across more than 200 countries. Google said it tied the scheme to Videostrong Technology, a Chinese company that was an Android original equipment manufacturer producing a range of screens, speakers and robots. The overwhelming majority of the infected devices in the X.CPE botnet are Android TV set-top boxes, Google said, adding that they observed a number of other infected Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signage devices. In lengthy reports about the scheme, Google and other cyber investigators accused Videostrong of monetizing the backdoor by “selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices.” “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” Google said. “We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.” Videostrong did not respond to requests for comment. The company says it has worked as an original equipment manufacturer for more than 14 years and sells a variety of AI-backed devices. Image: GoogleMillions of households Google said Videostrong was allegedly turning infected devices into a residential proxy network and loading other types of malware onto X.CPE-compromised devices. The botnet generated revenue from the devices by reselling bandwidth, data exfiltration, delivering video content, ad fraud, loading additional backdoors and installing apps for payment. The software allowed third-party traffic to pass through a person’s internet connection, using their internet address and bandwidth. X.CPE was embedded in the device’s firmware before it even reached a person’s home and was built to evade security checks. Videostrong allegedly continued to change the malware used, updating it in 2024 and 2026. Google worked with Japanese police, as well as cybersecurity firms TrendAI, Human and Synthient, to disrupt the domains that underpinned the botnet. “Our research identified over 1.3 million devices affected by this campaign,” said Robert McArdle, director of cybercrime research at TrendAI. “That's millions of households and businesses completely unaware that their equipment was being used as an accessory in active criminality — whether defrauding advertisers or piggybacking on their connections to carry out other attacks via residential proxies — which would commonly include identity theft impersonating people in their region.” According to Google, Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to pass its security tests and load the malware onto the devices. Google pledged to change its review process to stop future manufacturers from conducting similar campaigns. Google said it took legal action to take down the domains Videostrong used to control the botnet and install the malware while also suing to destroy the domains used by other malware families loaded onto the devices. But they noted that even if a user tried to uninstall the malware, it would automatically reinstall, according to cybersecurity researchers. The backdoor was able to silently download other files onto the device and execute them without user consent. Google did not explain if customers with infected devices will be notified or if there is any effort to forcibly remove malware from compromised devices as U.S. law enforcement agencies have done in other similar botnet cases. In response to questions about removing the malware, Charley Snyder, head of disruption operations at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told Recorded Future News that their actions severed the domains the botnet was communicating with, “effectively rendering the malware benign." Google claimed the takedown of command and control domains of Videostrong's criminal affiliates may have also cut off cybercriminal access to an additional 10 million compromised devices — many of which are not Android devices. Videostrong and any future subsidiaries are now banned from selling Android devices or supplying software to certified vendors, Google said. “The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase,” Google said. “Since at least late 2024, Videostrong has evolved its pre-installed malware from simple single-stage droppers into a modular, three-stage architecture designed for resilience and multi-tenant monetization.” Tech companies like Google have increasingly turned to court orders to take down malicious tools or services used to target their customers. Microsoft used court orders multiple times this year to destroy phishing platforms, malicious AI tools, and cybercrime-as-a-service infrastructure.
