1kxde0s.text: Large language model hijacking attacks, also known as LLMjacking, are generating large fraudulent cloud charges, with some organizations losing more than $100,000 per day. Companies can record costs as high as $1 million due to fraudulent calls using stolen API keys, researchers at Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant in analyzed incidents. Based on their observations, there are "two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure." The researchers identified two categories of threat actors: those who scan for publicly exposed LLM endpoints and those who steal valid API keys from unprotected machines. After gaining initial access, the attackers sell it to services known as LLM mixers, which provide their subscribers with unauthorized access to LLMs. Once access is resold, request volumes can spike suddenly, sometimes exceeding 1,000 requests per second. The service provider records the requests as legitimate consumption and charges the victim organization for the tokens. LLMjacking usage spike Source: Google GTIG and Mandiant observed an increase in this type of activity this year, with fraudulent charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, and cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1,000,000. LLM mixers offer access to AI resources at very low prices, using their proxy infrastructure to relay customers' prompts to hijacked services through stolen API keys. The researchers found several examples of such relaying infrastructure, including Jet Night, which sells “unlimited access plans” for $60/month, and the newapi[.]pro service. “Another threat actor that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours leveraged stolen third-party API keys to power the token routing service jet-night.com,” Google says. “Jet Night passed nearly one million dollars in token costs to the victim organization.” Jet Night pricing plans Source: Google Google also identified the threat cluster UNC6993, which appears to use gateway tools to aggregate stolen keys and distribute requests, and likely sells access via underground forums. The attackers gain access via exposed or compromised cloud credentials, service account keys, GitHub tokens, active session tokens, and LLM API keys. Attackers search the compromised environment for credentials, logs, databases, and secret managers, and try to create backdoor accounts or inject SSH keys to maintain persistent access. The researchers have also observed threat actors exploiting CVE-2026-40217, a vulnerability in LiteLLM that allows running arbitrary code on the server by leveraging the custom-code guardrail testing endpoint. In some cases, Google says that attackers used the victim's cloud infrastructure to host unauthorized proxy endpoints and agentic workloads. "For example, one threat actor enabled agents, deployed publicly accessible reverse proxies, and used custom Node.js proxy bundles to expose endpoints compatible with multiple frontier LLMs rebranded under a persona known as D1337-KAIROS," the researchers say. Google recommends several actions to protect against LLMjacking attacks, which start with prioritizing Identity and Access Management (IAM) and securing the supply chain. Companies should use centralized secrets platforms to enable the rotation and management of sensitive keys and secrets. Users should not have extended privileges unless required by their role and tasks. "Deny all permissions that are not explicitly required, including access to Cloud LLM services," Google recommends. Enforcing phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA), ensuring monitoring tools provide comprehensive visibility across the environment to identify unauthorized LLM and AI services (shadow AI), and setting API usage and spending limits can help organizations detect LLMjacking attacks early, limit their impact, or prevent them altogether. Furthermore, cloud audit and inference logs should be enabled and monitored for unauthorized service activation, suspicious credential checks, unusual usage, and attempts to disable logging. btvme7.text: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says North Korean hackers used a fake job interview to trick an employee into installing malware that ultimately let them compromise the company's wallet infrastructure and steal about $6.34 billion in digital assets. This new information was shared in an incident report published today, which details how the attackers used social engineering, malicious software, and compromised internal systems to carry out the October 29 crypto theft. As previously reported by BleepingComputer, the FBI attributed the attack to North Korean state-sponsored hackers known as TraderTraitor, also tracked as Lazarus Group, Jade Sleet, and APT38. Binance says the attack began in September when a software engineer was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform by someone impersonating a Project Director at a fictitious company. The employee's profile referenced his experience at Binance, making him a valuable target for attackers looking to breach the cryptocurrency exchange. The fake recruiter scheduled two interviews for the employee, first with someone posing as a human resources representative, then with another individual claiming to be the company's CEO. During the first interview, the fake HR representative held a live video call and shared a social media account with personal photos and videos to build trust. The second interview took place through a popular social chat application where the employee was instructed to download a coding assignment from an online code repository. According to Binance, the repository contained malicious code that, when executed, compromised the employee's device with previously unseen custom malware that antivirus software did not detect. "The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server," explained Binance. "The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time. The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging." Binance explained that the malicious script created a replacement executable named pyenv_ in the macOS Homebrew installation directory. The script then deleted the legitimate pyenv executable, renamed the malicious file to pyenv, modified its symbolic link, and used it to spawn a Z shell (zsh) process. The malicious replacement allowed the attackers to execute commands received from an attacker-controlled server. By October 20, the attackers had used the compromised engineer's computer and an internal AI tool to compromise two additional employees working on Binance's wallet infrastructure, obtaining credentials and a container deployment token. On October 29, the hackers used the stolen credentials to deploy a malicious script and gain unauthorized access to Binance's wallet signing service, allowing them to transfer billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains. The attackers also abused Ethereum's EIP-7702 authorization mechanism, allowing them to continue stealing cryptocurrency even after the exchange suspended withdrawals. Binance says it has since rebuilt affected systems, replaced compromised devices, and revoked stolen credentials. As of November 3, approximately $2.85 billion in stolen assets had been frozen or intercepted, while 98% of impacted token assets had been replenished as of October 31. Binance says it is continuing to investigate the breach and has brought in independent security firms to review its findings. Malicious job interviews Fake job interviews that lead to malware installs are a common tactic in North Korean hacking campaigns known as Contagious Interview and Operation Dream Job. These campaigns use fake job offers and interviews to trick developers and cryptocurrency employees into installing malware. In June 2025, cybersecurity firm Socket reported that a Contagious Interview campaign impersonated recruiters on LinkedIn and sent developers coding assignments containing malicious npm packages. As part of these attacks, the hackers distributed 35 malicious npm packages that installed malware, allowing them to steal browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data, and other information from infected computers. North Korean Lazarus hackers have also used similar tactics in Operation Dream Job, distributing malware disguised as employment documents to people working in software development and DeFi companies. While Binance has not linked the employee compromise to either specific campaign, the use of a fake recruiter, multiple interviews, and a malicious coding assignment closely mirrors these previously documented North Korean tactics. aznpxl.text: Developer platform WorkOS suffered a data breach after a threat actor accessed business contact records and summaries of customer communications. According to the company, the attacker used an AI offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts. Based on evidence from the investigation, no WorkOS app data or production services were accessed or affected. WorkOS is a developer infrastructure company that provides APIs, SDKs, and tools for integrating services such as enterprise authentication, single sign-on (SSO), user management, and identity management into applications. According to its website, at least 3,000 companies use its services, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, Perplexity, Snowflake, Plaid, Webglow, and Netlify. “On October 30, 2026, we identified unauthorized access to an internal WorkOS application used by our sales team,” the company says in an incident alert. Data accessed by the attacker includes: Business contact details (names, email addresses, job titles, and company affiliations from the CRM systems) Customer account histories (product usage and connection or directory health) Customer communications (summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations) Business account and relationship information (account histories, information about sales and customer relationship) After detecting the intrusion, WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application and reviewed its access controls on internal tools. The company also contracted an independent forensics and incident response firm to track the unauthorized activity and determine its full impact. The company promised to notify affected customers directly, and warned its users to remain vigilant for phishing or social engineering attempts leveraging the exposed information. ARTEX AI likely powering the attack WorkOS’s announcement says the attack used an AI-powered offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts. Company founder Michael Grinich shared more details, saying that the attacker used the ARTEX AI penetration testing suite that has been observed in multiple incidents this year. Released earlier this year by Chinese developers, the platform was available as an open-source project for offensive security. ARTEX AI became private after it was used in attacks targeting South Korean banks, but several forks of its code are still available. More recently, CrowdStrike revealed that cyber-espionage group “Vapor Panda” used the pentesting framework in a global campaign targeting 200 organizations. Previously, the non-profit cybersecurity organization DIVD also revealed that the same framework powered the attacks it suffered last September. Grinich explained that the investigating team identified user agents such as ‘artex-enrich/1.0’ and ‘norma/0.4’ in web requests from the threat actor. The founder assured that the cybersecurity incident has now been fully contained and promised to share more information about the attack after the investigation completes. 25ctq8.text: Multiple lawmakers and public figures in Germany are among the snooping victims Apple warned last week about spyware attacks, according to the country’s information security agency. The hacking attempts are a significant development underscoring the national security threat European officials face as spyware deployment becomes both increasingly visible and apparently inexorable under current policies on the continent. They also spotlight Europe’s continuing vulnerability to snooping, which human rights and digital freedoms advocates have loudly demanded lawmakers address more aggressively. On Monday, the German news magazine Der Spiegel reported the Apple threat notifications were sent to members of a German delegation of federal ministries’ staffers, lawmakers and journalists traveling with Chancellor Friedrich Merz on a sweep through Asia. While there Merz met with top officials in South Korea, Japan and Singapore. Many of the victims have not come forward, but on Tuesday morning, Franziska Brantner, co-leader of the Green Party and a member of the parliament’s European Affairs Committee, revealed she was among the victims, whom Apple said were located in 99 countries. The information security agency, known as the BSI, on Friday sent German officials, lawmakers and public figures who received the threat notifications a warning letter saying they should assume their devices are infected and immediately replace them, according to a local news outlet’s interview with Digital Minister Karsten Wildberg. The letter was sent within 24 hours of Apple sending the threat notifications, which Wildberg said highlights that the government “reacted super quickly.” The BSI said it does not know how many of the victims’ devices were actually infected versus merely targeted or why those receiving the alerts were pinpointed by hackers, but its announcement and letter alone make clear that it considers the attacks to be particularly noteworthy. Late last week, a Lebanese documentary filmmaker and Turkey-based reporter were the first victims to publicly confirm they were among scores, if not hundreds, of targets that received Apple warnings about spyware targeting. ‘Very different this time’ Hannah Neumann, a member of the European Parliament representing Germany, has long advocated for European lawmakers and officials to step up their efforts to combat spyware. She served on parliament’s PEGA committee — now disbanded — to investigate advanced commercial spyware, particularly the NSO Group’s frequently abused Pegasus software. In July, Neumann spoke out after spyware was discovered on the phone of a former parliamentarian who also sat on the investigating committee. The latest revelations further emphasize security threats advanced commercial spyware poses, she said. “Several foreign policy politicians and also staffers have received Apple notifications in the last round, and given that before it was maybe one in one round and then maybe another one in another round, this has been very different this time,” Neumann said in an interview. “There has been something big going on.” Neumann has long called spyware abuses a national security threat in addition to an invasion of privacy. “It's a hardcore security issue because once the technology is out there, we will see proliferation,” she said. “We will see more and more actors engaging in it, and they will not shy away from using it for political espionage reasons, and apparently now somebody has done that at a large scale against the German political elite.” A digital forensic researcher at the Citizen Lab pointed out that the attacks have become public on the eve of a Pall Mall Process meeting to be held in Paris on November 11-12, where voluntary industry guidelines for spyware usage will be unveiled. Pall Mall is an international initiative spearheaded by the French and British governments to stamp out the proliferation and abuse of spyware and other advanced surveillance technologies. “It wouldn’t shock me if the companies giving feedback at Pall Mall are among those captured by Apple’s latest threat notification round,” John Scott-Railton said via text. “What just happened in Germany is the latest proof that Europe has an untreated mercenary spyware epidemic,” he added. For too long, he said, European countries have tolerated spyware companies and signaled support for the technology by signing on as customers. “This is a very big deal and it proves that even the most technologically sophisticated European governments are totally vulnerable to mercenary spyware,” he said. “This is a chance for Germany to take decisive action to create serious deterrence and show leadership.” No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

boozc6.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 03, 2026Password Security / Incident Response Customers of the mSecure password manager are being urged to act now to protect the confidential information they store in it, possibly by changing passwords, resetting two-factor authentication (2FA), and removing passkeys. The warning came in an email sent on November 3 in the name of developer mSeven Software. It says the company recently learned of suspicious activity linked to the app but does not say what happened or whether anyone's stored data was exposed. The email says it went to current and former mSecure customers. A customer who received it posted its text in a thread on mSecure's support forum on November 3. As of 18:00 UTC on November 3, mSeven had posted nothing about the email on mSecure's X and Facebook accounts. No staff member had replied in that forum thread. The email says mSeven started an investigation, took steps to limit the problem and brought in outside cybersecurity experts. It does not name the systems involved, say when the activity happened or whether it has stopped, or give the number of people who received the email. mSecure can sync a customer's vault through mSecure Cloud, Dropbox, iCloud or Wi-Fi. The email does not say whether it matters which of these a customer uses. mSecure 7 can keep passkeys and 2FA codes in the vault next to passwords, on its Essentials plan and above. The email's advice is about protecting information stored in mSecure. The email does not say whether the 2FA and passkey steps cover those stored items, the mSecure account's own sign-in, or both. mSecure says vault data is encrypted on the customer's device before it is synced, and that even its developers cannot access customers' information. In mSecure 6.1.5 for Android, mSeven could, in theory, access stored data, according to Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), which found this in a study published in December 2025. The BSI tested only that version, and its results may have changed with later updates. The email does not say whether the suspicious activity reached vault data or the keys that protect it. What the Email Asks Customers to Do The email offers its steps as possibilities and does not say which accounts to deal with first or how to carry out each step. It also does not say whether customers should keep using mSecure, including to store their new passwords. As of 18:00 UTC on November 3, the newest iPhone version of mSecure in Apple's App Store was 7.1.0, released on October 23.

v3v437.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 03, 2026Data Breach / Cyber Attack Blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack on Tuesday disclosed that it was targeted in a cyber attack that allowed an unauthorized party to gain access to some parts of its infrastructure. The incident is assessed to be part of a large-scale, artificial intelligence (AI)-powered attack campaign that came to light last week. "An external attacker gained unauthorized access to part of Chainstack's infrastructure through a third-party component," the company said. "We detected the intrusion, cut the access paths, and are hardening our systems." According to the timeline of events shared by Chainstack, the attacker gained access to a development environment on October 26, 2026, and then escalated their access to break into "some parts of our production environment." The intrusion was subsequently detected on October 31, 2026, and the attacker's access was cut off that same day, the company noted. As part of the digital break-in, the threat actor is said to have accessed a database containing customer account information, including organization names, account holder names, the email addresses of organization’s members on Chainstack, and password hashes. "The attacker also had access to systems holding node credentials," Chainstack said. "We have no evidence they were read, but we are treating them as exposed and ask customers to rotate them." Besides rotating the node credentials, customers are advised to regenerate their platform API keys, update passwords -- including other services where the same password has been reused -- and remain alert to potential phishing attempts. Although Chainstack did not disclose any specifics about the attack, it's assessed to share overlaps with a campaign undertaken by a China-linked cluster to target high-value firms using ARTEX. WorkOS Targeted by ARTEX Too The development comes as API platform WorkOS also disclosed a security incident that involved the same autonomous AI agent framework to conduct offensive security operations. The incident, which was discovered on October 30, 2026, was limited to its GTM systems, and did not affect production systems or customer platform data. The accessed data includes - Business contact details (Names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, and company affiliations stored in its customer relationship management system) Business account and relationship information (Customer account histories and information about sales and customer-relationship information) Customer communications (Summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations) Operational metadata (Information about customers' use of WorkOS products, including product usage and connection or directory health) The breach is part of a growing trend in which AI agents are being employed to devise tailored attack strategies and automate different phases of the intrusion. "This increases the speed and scale of attacks that exploit weaknesses such as exposed applications and stolen credentials," WorkOS said. "It increases the need for timely remediation and monitoring that can connect suspicious activity across systems." Last week, blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis also revealed that it detected an "external actor using offensive agentic techniques" to obtain access to its systems and internal tools. As of November 2, 2026, the company has proactively taken its Reactor and Data Solutions products offline. "We are closely monitoring these systems for unusual activity and will keep you apprised of new information so you can make informed decisions for your business and operations," Chainalysis said. Another organization to be hit by ARTEX is the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD). The September 21, 2026, breach involved the exploitation of two zero-day flaws in the open-source Zammad ticketing system (CVE-2026-102489 and CVE-2026-102490), enabling attackers to escalate privileges, run code remotely, and exfiltrate data.

15i2z3v.text: Cryptocurrency giant Binance said North Korean hackers used a months-long attack involving multiple company employees to stage its headline-grabbing theft of $6.3 billion last week. The company released a post-mortem on Tuesday morning, outlining a campaign that dates back to June and involved the compromise of multiple employee devices. Binance CEO Richard Teng called it a “months-long campaign” that wasn’t the result of “one mistake or one breach.” “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign. It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” Binance said. “The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.” Investigators said the breach started in June, when an engineer downloaded malicious software to install a popular AI coding tool. Binance’s security team detected the malicious software and replaced the device but the hackers gained access to crucial information about the engineer and other people on the developer team. The company noted that throughout 2026, it has caught and stopped 57 separate attempts by North Korean actors to breach the company, compromise employees or break into corporate systems. These attempts involved fake job interview offers, malware disguised as developer tools, compromised browser extensions, malicious video conferencing tools and other social engineering campaigns. Started with one device By September, one of the campaigns was successful in compromising the device of a software engineer who was contacted for a fake job offer. During the second interview, the Binance employee was told to download an assignment that contained a malicious code repository. That download kicked off the attack that led to the theft, giving the hackers access to Binance systems and the ability to replace legitimate tools with malicious ones. The malware was not detected by Binance’s endpoint security protection tools, and the company said the attacker took further steps to conceal the malicious activity — removing traces of the initial compromise. By October 20, the hackers began to move laterally, using their access to the compromised device of the engineer to gain control of two other devices. The attackers successfully got into critical cryptocurrency wallet tools by October 29 and used credentials stolen from the breached employees to trigger the initial attack. Binance said the hackers used an internal wallet signing service to initiate the first transactions, which saw almost $400 million in various cryptocurrencies flow out of the platform. The company was alerted to the large transfers and began an investigation, but then $1.4 billion in bitcoin left the platform. The hackers used other mechanisms to conduct 50 other transactions that enabled the theft of $6.34 billion. Binance quickly coordinated with other platforms to freeze about $2.85 billion in assets and suspended withdrawals but could not stop millions more in funds from being stolen. The company said it lost valuable time in stopping the attack because it had to develop specialized procedures in the moment to revoke access and authorizations. “We have taken immediate action to contain the incident and strengthen the systems involved. The entry points identified as having been used in the attack have been closed,” Binance said. “Systems touched in the attack path have been rebuilt or replaced. We have also implemented tighter device controls, enhanced wallet-service risk controls and expanded AI-based behavioural anomaly detection.” Binance said it has taken several other actions to enable quicker responses to security incidents. All of the compromised devices and wallets have been replaced, while the credentials used in the attack have been decommissioned. It has also hired a security company to conduct a review of the incident to validate its findings and recommend additional actions. The tactics described by Binance resemble dozens of other attacks North Korean hackers have conducted over the last five years. Multiple cryptocurrency companies have reported laptops infected with malware as the source of breaches while Google and other cybersecurity firms have warned of North Korean campaigns using fake job interviews and exams as a way to gain entry to blockchain firms. Earlier this year, alleged North Korean groups stole $290 million from the Drift crypto platform in another sophisticated operation involving fake companies, alleged actors and more. North Korea denies role Over the weekend, the FBI and other U.S. agencies blamed the theft on North Korea’s TraderTraitor — a state-sponsored group that has spent years perfecting lucrative attacks on cryptocurrency exchanges and platforms. North Korean spokesperson Kim Yo Jong denied the country’s role in the attack on Monday, calling it an “absurd” effort to “damage the international image of the DPRK.” “It is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace, the wealth common to mankind, and resolutely reject any attempt to politicize the cyber issue and use it as a means of interfering in the internal affairs with other countries,” Kim said. The spokesperson eventually accused the U.S. of confiscating “illegally stolen cryptocurrency assets,” in an apparent reference to the Justice Department’s seizure of $15 billion worth of bitcoin from accounts allegedly linked to the chairman of a prominent Cambodian conglomerate who was indicted on charges that his company is behind a sprawling scamming empire. Blockchain security firms like Elliptic said the hackers have used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains to conduct about 40,000 transactions while shuffling funds to a new wallet every 25 seconds. Investigators from the United Nations and several other countries said North Korea has been responsible for stealing billions from cryptocurrency companies since 2017 — with much of the stolen money used to fund its sanctioned ballistic missile programs. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

jsmpyh.text: Three meat suppliers in Britain are among businesses that have been caught in a wave of cyberattacks across Europe targeting refrigeration systems, according to an industry trade body. Supermarket and grocery store refrigerator controls across Europe were hacked in the early hours of Monday in the second such wave of attacks in recent weeks — following a first wave in France — with unidentified perpetrators defrosting fridges and causing stock to spoil. The Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told Recorded Future News that its three affected members were attacked through vulnerable Copeland XWEB supervisory controllers. A Copeland spokesperson confirmed that certain XWEB monitoring solutions are impacted by the reported vulnerability. "We are continuing to assess the circumstances and have taken the appropriate actions based on the specific products involved," they said in a statement. "As part of our response, we have re-communicated the recommended patching and security protocols to ensure customers have the latest guidance to protect against the identified threats." AIMS spokesperson Tony Goodger described the association’s members as “collateral” because they ran the same software. None of the affected members lost meat, he said, but the incident “must act as a reminder to all in the food industry, at whatever point in the supply chain they are, that their businesses may be seen by some as targets.” No hackers have claimed responsibility for the attacks. British authorities say they have not attributed the incidents to any group, while a spokesperson for Belgium’s cybersecurity agency told Recorded Future News “it may never be possible to identify” who was behind them. Langridge Organic, a British fruit and vegetable wholesaler, told trade publication The Grocer that it had also been attacked. The company’s managing director Alex Pearce said it "was amazing how many parameters" the attackers had changed after accessing the controllers. Pearce said he was “pretty sure that I interrupted a live hacking event,” as he physically disconnected a fridge from the internet after observing it being remotely put into defrost mode. He said no stock was spoiled as a result of his team’s physical interventions. All of the British suppliers were reportedly using vulnerable temperature controllers for which a firmware update had been available since August. According to a security note shared among AIMS members, firmware for Copeland XWEB — version 1.12.1 and earlier — contained “severe authentication bypass vulnerabilities that allow hackers to take control without a password.” National impact ‘minimal’ says NCSC Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said Tuesday it was aware of the refrigeration attacks and assisting affected organizations. Its staff had worked through the night in an attempt to proactively contact companies that it detected had vulnerable systems exposed to the internet. Speaking at the launch of the agency’s annual report, Paul Chichester, its director of operations, said the impact was “minimal” so far. Richard Horne, NCSC’s chief executive, added that “although at a national level the impact is minimal, if you’re running the business that’s been hit by that, it is an enormous issue for you and your employees and everyone else.” The NCSC’s annual report raised the alarm about “the failure to implement even basic cyber protections” with Horne warning that Britain faced the “real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents” in the coming months. The businesses impacted in the fridge attacks appear to fit that pattern, given that they were running firmware that was known to be flawed. In August, researchers at industrial cybersecurity company Claroty disclosed almost two dozen vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB Pro controllers. In reference to the first wave of attacks in France, the NCSC said the attacks were not sophisticated. “This is using vulnerabilities that absolutely have been out there for a long period of time,” said Chichester. Horne said the attacks on freezers were “really just sort of the foothills” of the threat the agency was warning of in its report. “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that, in some ways, you could say are waiting to be exploited,” he said. Ollie Whitehouse, the agency’s chief technology officer, said he and his colleagues were “surprised to see some of these things being connected to the internet still in 2026, despite warnings that we have put out over the last couple of years.” AIMS is urging the government to give the food sector a stronger place in Britain’s designation of critical national infrastructure. No individual food sector assets are currently designated as critical under existing legislation. The sector is also not included under the forthcoming Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which would require the operators of essential services to maintain appropriate security measures — such as patching vulnerable systems promptly — or face a fine of up to £17 million ($22 million) or 4% of their global turnover for serious failures. The European Union’s counterpart legislation, NIS2, also covers food production and distribution. However, as reported by Politico, its breadth has drawn criticisms for potentially also catching “ice cream makers, Christmas lights manufacturers and German landlords.” No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

1y8zigo.text: Binance on Tuesday said the record-setting theft of $6.43 billion in assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange was the culmination of a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" that involved the use of a tampered Homebrew installation and recruitment-themed social engineering attack targeting two of its engineers. "It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident," the company said. "The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method." The starting point has been traced back to a supply chain attack targeting one of its engineers from the Wallet DevOps team (named "Engineer A"), who downloaded a trojanized Homebrew installer to install a popular artificial intelligence (AI) tool after searching for it on a search engine. The incident occurred in June 2026. Although Binance said it detected the attack and rotated all related credentials as a precautionary step, the company said information about "Engineer A's role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker." The second part of the attack occurred in September 2026, with the threat actor contacting another engineer (named "Engineer B") via a legitimate job-hunting platform by disguising themselves as a Project Director. The Project Director persona arranged a first-round interview with a human resources (HR) representative, which was then followed by a second-round interview with an individual claiming to be the CEO of a non-existent company. Binance did not disclose details of the fake company. Over the course of the first-round video interview, the HR representative shared a social media account, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in an attempt to build credibility and establish trust. The second round, on the other hand, took place on a popular social chat app. "Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an 'assignment' containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer," Binance said. "The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities." The undetected malware utilized advanced obfuscation and evasion techniques, including substituting a legitimate development tool component with a poisoned version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server. In addition, the threat actor took steps to cover up tracks by removing forensic artifacts related to the compromise. The intrusion moved to the next stage on October 20, 2026, when the adversary leveraged Engineer B's compromised computer and abused an internal AI tool to gain control over Engineer A and another Wallet Software Engineer C. "The attacker soon discovered Wallet DevOps Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer," Binance explained. "On 29 October between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Software Engineer C's computer, used the credentials stolen from Wallet DevOps Engineer A, deployed a container, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack." The attack ultimately exploited its unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process. In response to the incident, Binance has reconstructed the affected wallet system in a new environment, as well as rebuilt the internal AI tool and access controls. Other steps taken as of November 3 are listed below - Replaced affected devices. Decommissioned credentials and tokens related to affected engineers. Completed enhanced security scans across all employee devices. Enhanced AI-based behavioural anomaly detection. Strengthened wallet-service risk controls. Worked with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, and industry partners to trace and freeze affected assets. "The entry points identified as having been used in the attack have been closed. Systems touched in the attack path have been rebuilt or replaced," Binance said. "We have also implemented tighter device controls, enhanced wallet-service risk controls and expanded AI-based behavioural anomaly detection." "We are increasing investment in AI-enabled detection, endpoint protection, developer-environment security and behavioural anomaly monitoring." Since the start of the year, Binance is estimated to have foiled 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases, underscoring the persistent nature of the attacks targeting the cryptocurrency industry. "The techniques include fraudulent job interviews, malicious software disguised as popular developer tools, compromised software packages and browser extensions, fake video conferencing applications, and social engineering campaigns designed to steal credentials or deploy remote access malware," Binance said.

uxmlpx.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 03, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Barracuda has disclosed details of two vulnerabilities affecting its products that, if chained together, could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to a susceptible device. The vulnerabilities, a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability and a command injection vulnerability, have been assigned the CVE identifiers CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS score: 9.3) and CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS score: 8.6), respectively. While CVE-2026-116606 only affects Email Security Gateway, CVE-2026-111560 impacts the following Barracuda products - Email Security Gateway Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller Message Archiver WAF Control Center Web Application Firewall Web Security Gateway "Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product," Barracuda said. "If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device." Barracuda said that organizations that do not expose their administrative interfaces to the internet are less vulnerable to the attack path, urging customers to follow the steps below - Restrict access to administrative interfaces to trusted internal networksUse appropriate network access controls to limit exposure "Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches," it added. "If firmware on a device is multiple versions out of date, customers may need to perform more than one update."

1amhdkw.text: Google on Monday warned that threat actors are hijacking enterprise access to Large Language Models (LLMs) to fraudulently leverage expensive computing resources and AI services. The tactic is called LLMjacking, a form of resource hijacking adapted for the LLM era, where an attacker obtains an API key through phishing, source code leaks, misconfigured environments, or exposed client-side code to gain unauthorized access to an organization's LLM accounts, while the legitimate owner covers the consumption costs. Such attacks have a wide geographical footprint, with impacted entities located in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors. "Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked." On one end of the spectrum are low-level resource theft that involves the manipulation of customer support chatbots to conduct unauthorized tasks like code generation. LLMjacking is on the other end, as they target the backend model resources directly by identifying publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtaining valid LLM API keys. The most common initial access vector has been exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs), and active session tokens, which allow an attacker to establish an initial foothold into target organizations' infrastructure. This includes a threat actor called UNC6993, which is said to have breached a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used it to obtain access to an LLM API. "UNC6993 also hosted a session hijacking page masquerading as an application portal to join a group of LLM users," Google said. "This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls." In another case, an unknown attacker has been observed leveraging a stolen Personal Access Token to access private code repositories, following it up with the exploitation of a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running within a containerized cloud environment. Other initial access routes include the compromise of IAM credentials of corporate users to programmatically generate fresh access keys to bypass MFA safeguards, as well as the use of a hacked cloud Service Account key with broad project permissions and LLM API keys obtained from public GitHub repositories. Upon successfully gaining a foothold, the threat actors waste no time escalating privileges, burrowing deeper into the network, establishing persistence, and conducting internal reconnaissance to identify targets and further cloud credentials for lateral movement. Some of the observed tactics are listed below - Enumerate cloud services, code repositories, and data stores for sensitive credentials. Perform internal reconnaissance across multiple cloud regions to map available services and identity policies. Clone sensitive codebases to search for hard-coded secrets, configuration variables, and developer credentials. Scan access logs to identify credentials for secondary cloud environments. Run targeted database queries to harvest additional credentials. Abuse cloud identity permissions and virtual machine configurations to escalate privileges and maintain persistent access. Exploit token-creation privileges associated with service accounts to generate temporary credentials for high-privilege service accounts and exfiltrate infrastructure credentials, internal database passwords, and third-party API keys from cloud secret managers. Create unauthorized IAM and service accounts and inject SSH keys into compute instances for persistence. Create backdoor service accounts disguised as internal billing optimization utilities. Exploit vulnerabilities targeting LLM routing software, such as CVE-2026-40217 in LiteLLM, to escalate privileges. "The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming, and GPU hardware provisioning," Google said. "Threat actors also leveraged their access to host their own proxy endpoints and agentic workloads." UNC6993, for instance, has created additional API keys to scale their operations within victim cloud projects, racking up over $100,000 USD in billing charges. Some threat actors attempt to bypass rate limits by adopting a "burn and rotate" strategy that involves continuously creating and deleting short-lived service accounts The maturation of the LLMjacking ecosystem has also paved the way for the emergence of a new category of actors called LLM Mixers, highlighting a division of labor between attackers who establish initial access and those who manage downstream monetization infrastructure. LLM Mixers function as illicit routing gateways that proxy, aggregate, and resell unauthorized LLM access to other criminal actors via underground storefronts. One such service is Jet Night ("jet-night[.]com"), which offers an unlimited token plan with alleged access to a frontier model for approximately $60 per month. By fueling an illicit resale marketplace, it permits bad actors to siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected. Jet Night is far from the only token routing offering. According to a report published by Broadcom-owned Symantec and Carbon Black last week, there exists a grey market relay service that installs the genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code CLIs on enterprise systems, only to reconfigure them to route every request through third-party infrastructure instead of the vendors' own servers. The service is assessed to be active since at least early 2026, primarily impacting a dozen organizations located in Mainland China, along with multi-national subsidiaries based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia. Targeted sectors include industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals, and data center services. "Rather than building its own client software, the service repurposes the genuine CLI tools," Symantec said. "It installs them normally, then rewrites their configuration to switch sandboxing off, in Codex's case by setting it to 'danger-full-access,' and routes every request through its own servers instead of OpenAI's or Anthropic's." The service appears to mainly target markets where Anthropic and OpenAI do not operate, with the installation driven by an employee attempting to try out a Western AI coding assistant by turning to an unauthorized reseller. Notably, the service does not distribute a modified or trojanized client. Shortly after the legitimate install of the Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, users are likely instructed to run a one-line command to fetch fileless PowerShell or bash setup script from a lookalike domain ("vibe.aiok[.]me") that's used to override the configuration. The reconfiguration, which targets "~/.codex/config.toml" for Codex or "~/.claude/settings.json" for Claude Code, disables the CLI's execution sandbox, enables network access for the write sandbox, replaces the user's real API credentials with relay-issued tokens, and disables telemetry and error reporting. The script also checks the Windows locale setting to confirm it's running on a system in the region it serves before the setup is completed. It's suspected that the operators behind the service are not only circumventing regional restrictions imposed by Western AI vendors, but are also reselling capacity below market rates similar to Jet Night. Although there is no evidence to suggest that the service is abusing its position to harvest prompts entered by employees or fabricate or alter responses, the findings demonstrate the security risks associated with using such tools. "Threat actors will increasingly prioritize LLMJacking over traditional resource theft like cryptojacking, driven by the immediate, high-margin monetization enabled by emerging underground LLM Mixers," Google said. "As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware."

1u80jo1.text: An attacker broke into the update system of the cPGuard security tool on November 2 and used it to send a malicious script to customers' Linux servers. The script installed a backdoor and collected password hashes and other sensitive files from servers that ran it, cPGuard maker OPSSHIELD said in an advisory. The attacker has since taken some of that data. cPGuard 5.88.25 and later versions remove the backdoor and the files the script left. Credentials the script copied may still work after the update, so any server that may have run the script also needs new passwords and keys. At 02:06 UTC, the attacker, who has not been identified, used compromised credentials to get into cPGuard's update system. The script went out in cPGuard versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19. The attack was detected within 12 hours of those versions going out, according to OPSSHIELD. The company has cleared its infrastructure credentials and stopped the script from reaching more servers. It is still investigating how the attacker got the credentials. OPSSHIELD has not said how many servers installed one of these versions. Servers check for updates at intervals, so some may not have run the script. Admins can check whether a server installed an affected version by searching its update log: grep 'Successfully updated' /opt/cpguard/logs/install_log An entry for any version from 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 means the server installed an affected update. The entry alone does not show that the script ran or that data left the server. The server should still be treated as potentially compromised, even if it now runs 5.88.25 or later. A server with no matching entries, or with a missing or incomplete log, may still have run the script. Admins who are unsure can contact OPSSHIELD Support. The script collected these kinds of data, OPSSHIELD found: /etc/shadow and /etc/passwd, root's MariaDB or MySQL configuration (my.cnf), root's shell history, and the SSH authorization and known-hosts files for root. It may not have collected every file from every server, and the company is still working out what left each one. The /etc/shadow file stores one-way password hashes. Weak, common or previously leaked passwords can be recovered from those hashes by testing guesses offline, and even strong ones still need resetting. Secrets that may sit in the database configuration or shell history have no such hashing to protect them. The script uploaded what it collected to a licensing server run by OPSSHIELD itself, using a compromised account, so the attacker could pick it up later. OPSSHIELD has since secured that account. The attacker took 32 files from that server, each tied to one customer server, OPSSHIELD estimated late on November 2 UTC. The count covers only files known to have been taken, and it may change. It does not show how many servers may be involved in total. Beyond the data collection and the backdoor, OPSSHIELD has found no other malicious activity so far, a finding it says is not final. What cPGuard Admins Should Do Now OPSSHIELD asks admins to update every cPGuard server now and confirm the version: Run cpgcli update --start on each server. Run cpgcli --version and check that it reports 5.88.25 or later. If the update fails or the version is lower, contact OPSSHIELD Support. Admins should also take these steps for any server where the script ran or may have run: From a trusted recovery environment, reset the passwords for root and every other local Linux account that uses a password. From a trusted device, change any of those passwords that are also used on other systems. Rotate the server's database passwords, S3 access keys, DigitalOcean tokens and any secrets recorded in root's shell history. Replace the SSH private keys stored under /root/.ssh, and remove the matching old public keys from every system that trusts them. OPSSHIELD is not recommending a full reset or operating system rebuild as a routine step, and says that view could change as the investigation continues. Admins who find other signs of compromise, or cannot confirm a server is clean, should ask OPSSHIELD Support for a case-by-case review, which may lead to a rebuild. Separately, OPSSHIELD is releasing another update, as a precaution, that removes its support-access keys from cPGuard servers where they were added earlier. Support access is a cPGuard feature customers use to let OPSSHIELD staff into a server for troubleshooting. Granting it adds an SSH public key belonging to OPSSHIELD to the authorized_keys file for root, according to the company's documentation. OPSSHIELD has not said whether the private key that matches its support-access key was exposed in the attack. Files the Script Left Behind OPSSHIELD published these file names. The update removes the backdoor shell and the collection directory, so their absence after updating proves nothing about whether the script ran. File: cpguard-v58812-i91511.sh (the malicious script) File: /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh (backdoor shell) Directory: /var/tmp/.cpg91511 (where the script gathered files) File: /var/tmp/.cpg91511/loot.tgz (archive the script prepared)
